articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026 live — the Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 are all official
articles.text:
Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026 live — the Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 are all official
We're live from Samsung's big day for foldables and more
Samsung's second big phone launch of the year is now over — and as expected, at the July edition of Unpacked 2026 saw the launches of several new Fold and Flip phones, plus the full reveal of Samsung's new Intelligent Eyewear smart glasses.
Leading Samsung's new foldables range are the new Z Fold 8 Ultra, passport-style Z Fold 8, and the updated Z Flip 8. The highlight, at least among the crowd, was the Z Fold 8, which likely gives us a hint of what to expect from the rumored iPhone Ultra.
But the most intriguing new devices were the range Intelligent Eyewear smart glasses, which Samsung's made in collaboration with Google. These will come in a range of designs when they launch "this Fall", from classic square and round-style frames to cat-eye-style silhouettes, and we've already had an early look at them.
You can read everything that happened at Samsung Galaxy Unpacked's July 2026 edition below. Which device are you most excited about? Make sure you also vote in our poll below...
Read all of our Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026 coverage
- I’ve spent an hour with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra — and I need to upgrade my Z Fold 7 ASAP
- I went hands-on with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and this passport-shaped oddity has revived my interest in foldable phones
- 'Finally, we've got silicon-carbon' — why SuperSaf is just as excited as we are for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's new battery
- 'If, because of that, we stop innovation, we don’t go anywhere': we got a first look at Samsung Intelligent Eyewear, the smart glasses entering a fraught market worried about privacy
- I've tested the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8, and its new camera features make it an excellent vlogging camera alternative — so long as you don't mind the middling image quality
- Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 review: slimmer, lighter, better
- I've found all the best Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Z Fold 8 preorder deals — where to get the biggest trade-in rebates and discounts
That's a wrap
So that's it for Samsung's second Galaxy Unpacked event of the year. We've already been hands-on with all of the devices, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear.
There weren't many surprises given the leaks were so generous, but we did all the official pricing — and the hikes aren't quite as bad as many feared. Samsung's Intelligent Eyewear (surely they're going to get a snappier nickname) also looks very interesting, if it can navigate the Great Smartglasses Backlash.
It's time for smart glasses
As expected, Samsung's 'one more thing' at Unpacked is its Intelligent Eyewear — and it does looks pretty impressive.
Samsung has partnered with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker in its attempt to take on the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which is something we already knew. But we've just learned a bit more about their design and specs, including a new hinge design that has a power slider next to it.
Samsung is claiming nine hours of battery life from a single charge with 'mixed use' — which is seemingly around 90 minutes of notifications, 30 minutes of calls, 35 AI conversations, 12 message read alouds, 60 minutes of music playback, nine photo captures, and three one-minute videos.
It also says you'll be able to charge them more than seven times overs using their case. They'll apparently be lighter than most AI glasses (although their exact weight is still TBC) and will be powered by a Snapdragon AR1 chipset.
The Intelligent Eyewear (surely there's a snappier name) will launch in the Fall, so sometime between September and November. But a big question remains unanswered, how much will they cost?
Google talks Gemini
Google's Rick Osterloh has stepped in to tell us about the Gemini features that'll be available on Samsung's new foldables — and its new smart glasses too.
Gemini Notebook (the new name for NotebookLM) will apparently come preinstalled on the new foldables and buyers will get six months of Google AI Pro too (after which, you'll have to pay, of course).
Gemini Intelligence will also be coming to new smartglasses from Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker — and we're about to hear more about those...
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 looks hardcore
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is here — it looks pretty similar to its predecessor from a couple of years ago, but there are quite a few upgrades under the hood.
Its engine is the new Snapdragon Elite processor, which apparently offers 32% better performance than before. The Watch Ultra 2 is also the toughest Samsung watch so far, with IP69K and 10 ATM waterproof ratings.
There are some pretty hardcore diving features too, including Samsung's own diving algorithm and nitrogen absorption monitoring. Basically, Samsung is gunning for Garmin here.
The Watch Ultra 2 starts at $699 with the Galaxy Watch 9 starting at $379, with the Watch Ultra 2 launching from August 7.
Enter the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
It's time to move onto smartwatches. Samsung's just revealed the Galaxy Watch 9, and it's promising some handy new software features.
These include sleep apnea detection, which is also coming to the Galaxy Ring — and apparently makes it the only FDA-cleared, over-the-counter ring device with that feature.
The Galaxy Watch 9 will also have "proactive" features that constantly monitor things like heart rate and heart rate variability, and crunch all these together into a new heart health score.
Samsung says it's partnering with iFit for its subscription fitness content, too. But the more exciting smartwatch is coming next...
Spider-Man drops in
A Spider-Man interlude has just broken up the foldables news, as we get a teaser from his newest movie plus a chat from Ned, who's shown off a 'Spidey Tracker' alongside camera footage from the Z Fold 8 Ultra.
It's back to reality now though, as Samsung moves onto Samsung Care+ and the Galaxy Card, its new Apple Card rival that was announced this week.
Samsung's 'thinnest Flip yet'
This should be the final foldable from today's Unpacked — Samsung's Lee Dunham has just announced the Z Flip 8, and it sounds like a decent upgrade.
There's seemingly a much better Flex Display experience, with boosts to Now Brief (including the option of adding your own custom cards). And it's a bit slimmer and lighter at only 6.1mm thick when folded, and weighing in at 180g. You also get the same ProVisual engine as you get on Samsung's other Galaxy phones.
The downside is that pricing for the Z Flip 8 starts at $1,199 (with pre-orders starting today), which means it's a bit pricer than last year.
Telephoto out, 'FanCam' in
Sadly, there's no telephoto camera on the Z Fold 8, which is a shame — but Samsung's seemingly quite proud of its new 'FanCam' feature.
This new AI feature helps you quickly edit videos into your choice of aspect ratio, while keeping the star of your video in the center of the frame. Pretty neat, if perhaps not as useful as a telephoto — though that's probably revealing of Samsung's target market for the Z Fold 8.
Now onto the Z Fold 8
This is the one most of us have been waiting for — Samsung's revealed its new passport-style Fold 8, and it got more of a reaction from the crowd than the Ultra.
Samsung's explaining the benefits of that more square display, claiming it bring "a whole new dimension to mobile gaming", while in portrait the 3:4 ratio makes it a good fit for reading.
I definitely like the form factor (in theory), and it's likely a hint of what Apple's going to bring with the iPhone Ultra. It's also apparently the "world's lightest fold" ever...
Camera boosts for the Z Fold 8 Ultra
Samsung is now talking cameras on the Z Fold 8 Ultra, leaning heavily on its Nightography skills and talking up its much-improved 50MP ultrawide camera.
It also has a 200MP main camera with an f/1.7 lens and a 10MP telephoto that gives you up to 3x optical zoom, which are similar to its Fold 7 predecessor.
First up, the Z Fold 8 Ultra...
Samsung's starting its Z Fold 8 Ultra promo with Flex Titanium, the new hinge design it announced last week that promises to make the crease less visible.
Also, there's battery news — it has largest-ever battery in a Galaxy Z Fold phone (at 5000mAh), and for the first time uses silicon carbon tech that we've seen in its many Chinese rivals — hooray...
AI and privacy are the hot topics
Samsung's TM Roh is on the stage right now talking about the "the importance of AI infrastructure", as he says Galaxy AI will be coming to 800 million devices by the end of the year. Now we're moving onto its foldables, starting with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra...
The Samsung Glasses are coming
That's a surprise, Samsung has just teased that the Galaxy Glasses are coming at today's event. But first, it's going hard on security and privacy...
And we're off
TechRadar's Phones editor Axel Metz has some final pre-Unpacked thoughts as we go through Samsung's pre-amble.
"I’m curious to see whether Samsung positions the shorter, wider Galaxy Z Fold 8 as its hero product this year — i.e. the foldable it hopes and expects people to buy — or simply as a more affordable alternative to the premium Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra," he says.
"In making the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung is acknowledging that the taller, narrower form factor of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra isn’t very ‘Gen Z’, and with Apple rumored to be releasing a similarly sized iPhone Ultra later this year, I — and probably Samsung — expect this new aspect ratio to become the foldable mainstream. Where does that leave the Ultra in years to come?" he says.
Get your popcorn ready
We're just a minute away from the start of Unpacked, and the expected arrival of its new foldables and smartwatches.
A final thought from TechRadar's Editor at Large, Lance Ulanoff, who's at the event right now. "What may be missing from this event is any kind of surprise. Samsung is very leaky, and most of the excitement tends to be muted by the time they tell us what we already knew or read about somewhere," he says.
"For Samsung, the goal is to generate Apple-level energy for its latest foldables and any other products they pull out of their back pocket. It's especially important to build that kind of momentum before Apple begins its product rollout juggernaut in September," he adds.
Five minutes to go...
It's now just five minutes till kick off, and TechRadar's Lance Ulanoff has shared some final thoughts on this year's second Unpacked.
"We pretty much all know the shape of things to come, but I'm super curious to see the reaction from the crowd here and online. Is different better or just different? Can more fold shapes expand the market? Or can only Apple do that?" he says.
We won't have to wait long to find out...
What about the Galaxy Ring 2?
What's TechRadar's Senior Fitness & Wearables Editor Matt Evans most excited about at today's Unpacked?
"I'm most looking forward to the wearables — the Watch 8 was outstanding last year, and I’m hoping for more of the same on that front. But the hotly-rumored Watch Ultra 2 is going to be the real star. Plus, who knows? We may event get a hint about a Ring 2…", he says.
Samsung has already confirmed it's working on the Galaxy Ring 2 — and while it isn't expected to get a full launch today, we could well get a teaser at the end of the event (just as Samsung did for the original Ring).
A subtle hint?
We're taking our seats at London's Galaxy Unpacked 2026 event and noticed a nice little touch from Samsung.
When you remove the perforated portion of our lanyards, it's remarkably close to the expected shape of the Z Fold 8 that we've seen in leaks.
Still, if you want an even clearer idea of what's coming, check out the leaked marketing materials that have just landed for the Fold 8 series. Or you could just wait 15 minutes to see the real thing...
These last-minute leaks are looking quite official
We're now less than 30 minutes away from Samsung Galaxy Unpacked 2026, and the leaks are looking ever more convincing, with what appears to be official marketing imagery having now leaked too, as you can see above.
This shows off all three expected foldables — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8.
The purple Z Fold 8 Ultra looks quite appealing, but hopefully the pink background is a sign that we'll get some brighter colors too.
Samsung's first smart glasses sound like Ray-Ban Meta rivals
Samsung could be about to make smart glasses more mainstream, as its first pair is rumored to be included in today's announcements, and the Samsung Galaxy Glasses as we're calling them for now have been extensively leaked.
A detailed new leak on WinFuture tallies with what we've heard before, including that these apparently won't have a screen, and will instead rely on cameras and access to Gemini, which should be able to see what you can.
They sound a lot like the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and like those they apparently use a Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chipset, which is now three years old. Still, with supposedly 9 hours of battery life, Gemini access, and a big brand name behind them, they could be a hit.
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 might live up to its name
We're also expecting various wearables today, and WinFuture has spilled the beans on the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 and Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 in a detailed leak.
The latter could have a slightly larger and much brighter display than its predecessor, coming in at 1.52 inches and 5,000 nits, and joined by a colossal — by smartwatch standards — 800mAh battery, along with a build that's designed with divers in mind.
This is sure to be expensive, but the standard Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 should be a cheaper option for anyone who doesn't need all the bells and whistles offered by the Ultra. Sadly though we're not expecting a new Classic model this year.
All the specs have already leaked
Samsung might not have too many surprises today if you've been following the leaks and rumors, as WinFuture.de recently leaked complete specs lists for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8.
Highlights if this leak is accurate include a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset for the two Z Folds and — at least in Europe — an Exynos 2600 for the Galaxy Z Flip 8.
We'll also apparently get a higher-capacity and faster charging 5,000mAh / 45W battery in the Z Fold 8 Ultra, but the real highlight could be the base Z Fold 8, since this is widely expected to have a new shorter, wider form factor, which according to this leak will allow for a 7.6-inch foldable screen and a 5.5-inch cover display.
A self-healing crease?
Samsung's upcoming foldables might not just have smaller creases than their predecessors, they could also have self-healing ones if the latest leak (above) is to be believed.
It's unclear how this would work, but perhaps it would ensure the crease doesn't become more visible over time. It also reminds us of the self-healing finish on the LG G Flex series, which could automatically fill in minor scratches.
It will be interesting to see how Samsung's take on this works, but if this leak is accurate then it could be Samsung's secret weapon against the upcoming foldable iPhone Ultra.
Brace yourself for price hikes
Some slightly less positive news from today's Galaxy Unpacked 2026 event is likely to be price hikes for the Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8.
A recent report from Korea (via Phone Arena) suggested that both foldables could be about $130 pricier than their predecessors. In the grand scheme of RAMageddon, that wouldn't be too bad — and the Fold and Flip series have never been the most affordable phones anyway.
Samsung has also already increased the prices of the Z Fold and Flip 7 series over the past year, so hopefully that will soften today's potential price rises...
If you host an event in London...
The umbrellas are already out at the Galaxy Unpacked 2026 queue. We've had what feels like months without rain in London, but right on queue the dark clouds are forming.
It's now just over 90 minutes till kick-off time, so hopefully we'll be ushered inside soon...
Will Samsung finally solve foldable creases?
There's a good chance that we'll see another big step towards crease-free foldables today. We recently visited Samsung Display's secret labs where it talked to us, among many other things, about its new "Flex Titanium Technology".
This includes a special structure at the fold to give added flexibility and help reduce crease visibility. We've recently more leaks on that theme — and while the image above doesn't look like a particularly fair comparison in terms of lighting, I'm hoping this new feature lives up to the hyper when we see it in person later.
We've landed at Unpacked
We're very keen here at TechRadar, so we've already arrived at the Galaxy Unpacked event in London, and it's very... quiet.
That's understandable, as we're still two hours away from kick-off and many international attendees will be coming from hotels much closer to the start time.
A London-based Unpacked is a rarity — last year, Samsung did a mix of US-based and virtual events, while this year's earlier Unpacked in February was in San Francisco.
You have to go back to 2012 for the last time London hosted Samsung's main event, which saw the arrival of the Galaxy S III...
What are you most excited to see?
We've done a full rundown of everything we're expecting to see at Unpacked 2026, so that's worth a read as we get closer to kick-off (in just over two hours).
But the short version is that we're expecting three foldables (a Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8), plus two Galaxy Watches (the Watch Ultra 2 and Watch 9), and (potentially) also Samsung's first smart glasses.
Which one are you most excited about? Let us know in the poll below...
The Z Fold 8 is winning the hype battle
The Galazy Z Fold 8 is emerging as the potential star of today's Unpacked event — and the foldable has just appeared in a new teaser poster (above).
It's the Z Fold 8's wider, passport-style design, which will likely separate it from the taller Fold 8 Ultra, that makes it the one I'm most interested in from today's launches. Partly because it also probably gives us an early peak of the iPhone Ultra's likely form factor.
We're expecting to see a 5.5-inch cover display and 7.6-inch inner display, both with a 120Hz refresh rate. The teaser poster matches some of the leaked dummy units that we saw earlier this year (below).
Welcome to Galaxy Unpacked 2026 (the sequel)
Hello, and welcome to our liveblog for Samsung's second big phone launch of the year, Galaxy Unpacked 2026.
We'll be reporting live from the London event, which kicks off at 9am ET / 6am PT / 2pm BST / 11pm AEST. But first, it's time to take you through all of the last-minute rumors on what we're expecting to see — and we certainly haven't been short of leaks...

articles.title: Borrow the speed, keep the discipline: Zoho's startup playbook for MSMEs
articles.text:
Borrow the speed, keep the discipline: Zoho's startup playbook for MSMEs
On the opening day of MSME Sparks 2026, Zoho's global startup head broke down how India's MSMEs can borrow the best of startup culture while staying anchored to the fundamentals that have always kept them standing.
India is home to 5.93 crore MSMEs, contributing to 30% of the country's GDP, 45% of its exports, and employment for over 25 crore people. They are, in every sense, the quiet engines behind India's growth story. Recognising this, YourStory launched MSME Sparks 2026, a five-day celebration that ran virtually from June 22-25 and culminated in a grand finale on June 26 at ITC Gardenia, Bengaluru.
Built around the idea of Bharat powering the world, the initiative brought together founders, policymakers, and ecosystem enablers to spotlight the resilience and ambition driving India's enterprise economy. It was organised around six themes: digital transformation, access to capital, sustainability, going global, policy and compliance, and what's next in AI and data-led innovation.
On the first day of the virtual edition, one keynote session tied several of these threads together. Titled ‘Borrow the speed, keep the discipline: A startup playbook for MSMEs’, the session featured Gautam Varma, Global Head, Zoho for Startups, exploring how MSMEs can adopt the agility of startups without losing the financial discipline that has kept them standing for decades.
Varma opened by flipping the popular narrative around startup success on its head. "There is a significant part about the entire startup story that nobody posts about," he said, pointing to data from Startup Genome and Carta showing that 74% of high-growth startups attribute their failure to premature scaling. In 2024, one startup shut down after a year in business; by 2025, that figure had surged to seven.
His central message was simple. MSMEs do not need to copy the startup model wholesale. They need to borrow its engine while keeping their own chassis intact.
"All I need to do is to borrow the engine, take data decisions, fast experiments, tech-enabled scale, run it by a very fast feedback loop, and then layer it on top with AI to enable speed while retaining my core chassis, which is cash discipline, profitability, long-term thinking, and deep customer trust," he said.
Much of this tension, Varma argued, plays out inside generational businesses, where the friction between old and new ways of working often surfaces not in boardrooms but at the dinner table. He cited data showing that 40% of next-generation members entering family businesses feel frustrated trying to push digitalisation, while nearly 45% of current owners do not expect their children to simply run the business as is. The resolution, he said, lies in finding common ground around hard numbers, since margins and pricing are facts both generations already agree on.
In his view, technology's role is to organise and surface shared data so decisions can be made faster and with less friction.
To ground the discussion, Varma walked through the journey of Tulsi Weigh Solutions, a 70-year-old, Kolkata-headquartered company serving over 6,200 customers across 15 countries without ever raising external funding. The business moved its operations on to Zoho One in 2022, consolidating CRM, finance, HR, and collaboration tools into one ecosystem.
While individual teams gained better control, the founder still lacked a single, bird's-eye view of the business. The next step was connecting that consolidated data to an AI layer, letting the founder ask plain English questions such as renewal rates by region or conversion rates on recent leads, and get instant, contextual answers across the business.
Closing the session, Varma offered MSMEs three practical steps: convert one gut decision into a data decision, run a small experiment based on it, and let AI work on existing business data with proper guardrails in place.
He left the audience with a sharp closing line. "Speed without discipline is just a faster way to run out of money," he said, adding that an MSME's real strength is not size or adaptability but longevity itself. "It's not that you're small and then you're adaptable. It's that you're still here."
The session set the tone for what followed across MSME Sparks 2026's opening day: a recurring reminder that technology, and AI in particular, is no longer a differentiator reserved for a few, but a growth lever increasingly available to every MSME willing to use it.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft va intégrer Copilot dans l’Explorateur de fichiers
articles.text:
Vous pensiez en avoir assez vu avec Copilot dans Windows 11 ? Accrochez-vous, ce n’est pas encore terminé. Microsoft a visiblement l’ambition d’intégrer son assistant IA directement dans l’Explorateur de fichiers de son système d’exploitation.
Bien que la firme de Redmond s’est engagée à faire un peu de ménage pour ce qui l’intégration de l’IA au sein de ses applications, cela ne signifie pas pour autant qu’elle souhaite l’abandonner définitivement. Bien au contraire.
Copilot pourra analyser vos fichiers dans l’Explorateur
Dans la build 28000.2605 de Windows 11 26H1 publié dans le canal Release Preview, Microsoft a déployé un certain nombre de nouveautés concernant l’Explorateur de fichiers.
Désormais, lorsque vous survolez un fichier avec la souris depuis la page d’Accueil de l’Explorateur de fichiers, de nouvelles commandes rapides s’affichent. Vous pouvez, par exemple, choisir d’Ouvrir l’emplacement du fichier. Mais Microsoft a aussi intégré une nouvelle commande Copilot permettant de demander à l’IA d’analyser le fichier en question directement au sein d’une fenêtre de discussion.
Pour le reste, Microsoft s’est attachée à optimiser les performances de l’Explorateur de fichiers. Celui-ci s’ouvre en principe plus rapidement et sa réactivité est meilleure lors du montage d’images disques. Microsoft précise par ailleurs que la barre d’adresse prend désormais en charge les chemins contenant des doubles antislashs ou des guillemets.
La firme de Redmond a également travaillé sur la liste déroulante des suggestions de la barre d’adresse qui affiche désormais des résultats plus fiables et se ferme dorénavant systématiquement dès lors qu’un élément est sélectionné. Microsoft en a aussi profité pour résoudre un bug où les fichiers OneDrive pouvaient apparaître en double dans la section Favoris sur la page d’Accueil.
Ces nouveautés ayant été publiées dans le canal Release Preview, celles-ci pourraient être déployées dans le canal stable très prochainement, probablement avec le prochain Patch Tuesday.

articles.title: 3 neue Gemini-Modelle, aber 1 fehlt
articles.text:
Google bringt drei neue Gemini-Modelle an den Start – aber ein wichtiges Update fehlt
Eigentlich wollte Google sein neues Flaggschiff-Modell Gemini 3.5 Pro schon im Juni 2026 veröffentlichen. Offenbar verhindern Performance-Probleme den angekündigten Launch, wie es aus internen Quellen heißt. Demnach soll die KI vor allem beim Coding deutlich hinter der Konkurrenz von Anthropic und OpenAI zurückliegen.
Gemini: Drei neue Modelle für KI-Agenten
Statt Gemini 3.5 Pro hat Google jetzt drei andere Versionen seiner Gemini-KI an den Start gebracht: Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite und 3.5 Flash Cyber. Alle drei Modelle sollen vor allem für Nutzer:innen geeignet sein, die in größerem Umfang KI-Agenten erstellen und betreiben. Die aktuellen Modelle sollen besonders in puncto Effizienz, Latenz und Zuverlässigkeit punkten.
Gemini 3.6 Flash etwa soll gegenüber dem Vorgängermodell 17 Prozent weniger Token verbrauchen und damit deutlich günstiger zu betreiben sein. Dennoch sei die Performance bei Coding, Wissensarbeit und multimodalen Fähigkeiten laut Google gestiegen.
Spezielles Modell für Cybersicherheit
Das im Hinblick auf Kosten effizienteste Modell ist derweil Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, wie es bei Techcrunch heißt. 3.5 Flash Cyber wiederum richtet sich an Regierungen und als besonders vertrauenswürdig eingestufte Partnerfirmen. Denn dieses Modell ist vor allem auf das Finden und Schließen von Sicherheitslücken ausgerichtet – und das bei vergleichsweise geringen Kosten.
Der Launch von gleich drei neuen KI-Modellen kann allerdings das Offensichtliche nicht verbergen – die Probleme bei Gemini 3.5 Pro. Google erklärt dazu, dass das Modell derzeit noch mit Partnern getestet werde und es – „sobald es fertig ist“ – verfügbar gemacht werde. Einen konkreten Termin für die Veröffentlichung nannte Google nicht.
Google arbeitet schon an Gemini 4
Ohnehin, so Google, werde intern schon längst an Gemini 4 gearbeitet. Dafür habe man den „bisher ambitioniertesten Pre-Training-Run“ gestartet. Intern sei man „begeistert vom Fortschritt“. Genauere Angaben fehlen aber auch hier.
Währenddessen schläft die Konkurrenz nicht. Seit dem letzten großen Gemini-Pro-Update im Februar 2026 hat OpenAI GPT-5.5 veröffentlicht und mit dem Rollout von GPT-5.6 begonnen. Anthropic brachte Clauce Opus 4.8 und Sonnet 5 an den Start. Außerdem bekommen immer mehr Nutzer:innen Zugriff auf das Fable-5-Modell.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Unpacked (julio 2026): sigue la presentación de los nuevos plegables de Samsung en directo con nosotros [finalizado]
articles.text:
| El evento ha finalizado. Aquí tienes todo lo que ha presentado Samsung. | 
Si hay una cita que marca el ecuador del verano esa es, sin duda, el Unpacked de Samsung. La compañía coreana nos reúne todos los veranos para presentar sus nuevos dispositivos (plegables, no es ningún secreto por dónde van los tiros) en un evento que apunta maneras. El año pasado fue en Nueva York, este año es en Londres y, como no podría ser de otra forma, podrás seguirlo en vivo y en directo con nosotros.
El Galaxy Unpacked tendrá lugar hoy, miércoles 22 de julio, a las 15:00 hora peninsular española. Podrás seguirlo en vivo a través de nuestro canal de YouTube, de nuestra página de directos y de nuestro perfil de Instagram. Los horarios según regiones son los que siguen:
- España: 15:00 (14:00 en Canarias).
- México: 7:00 AM

articles.title: Tom Hiddleston recommande de regarder la série Loki avant Avengers: Doomsday
articles.text:
La première bande-annonce d’Avengers: Doomsday, qui affole déjà les compteurs, a confirmé ce que beaucoup craignaient. Pour apprécier le film à sa juste valeur, il faudra avoir vu plusieurs films et séries du Marvel Cinematic Universe, voire des contenus encore plus anciens (les films X-Men de la Fox, par exemple). C’est potentiellement un vrai souci, puisque certaines clés de compréhension pourraient échapper à une partie du public.
On espère donc que les scénaristes d’Avengers: Doomsday ont évité certains écueils, en facilitant au maximum l’intégration des nombreux personnages qui nourrissent l’intrigue. Néanmoins, il faut prendre conscience qu’il faudra avoir vu et digéré certaines choses avant d’aller au cinéma. À ce sujet, l’acteur Tom Hiddleston, qui prête ses traits à Loki, partage un conseil dans les colonnes de TechRadar, le 21 juillet 2026.
Conseil : regardez Loki avant d’aller voir le prochain Avengers
« Si vous ne l’avez pas encore vue, allez-y. Et si vous ne l’avez pas revue avant Doomsday, allez la revoir », sourit Tom Hiddleston quand on lui demande s’il est nécessaire d’avoir vu Loki avant Avengers: Doomsday. Il prêche bien évidemment pour sa paroisse, tant il est fier de la série diffusée en exclusivité sur Disney+. Il argumente : « Je dis toujours aux gens qu’il faut qu’ils regardent Loki. Je suis vraiment fier de cette série — j’y ai mis toute mon âme et j’adore incarner Loki (…). C’était une expérience tellement agréable, parce que toute la série tourne autour de l’identité, de la quête de sens et de l’appartenance, mais aussi du temps, de la façon dont nous le percevons et de la meilleure manière de l’utiliser. »
Loki apparaît dans la bande-annonce d’Avengers: Doomsday, lui qui s’est offert une porte de sortie narrative après sa mort dans Avengers: Infinity War (tué par Thanos). Il est devenu le héros d’une série centrée sur le TVA, le bureau des anomalies temporelles, chargé de veiller à la bonne santé du multivers. Dans la prochaine réunion des super-héros Marvel, il est attendu que Loki soit — en partie — à l’origine du retour de Steve Rogers, resté dans le passé pour vivre une retraite amoureuse auprès de Peggy Carter. Loki enverrait toute la famille sur la Terre des Quatre Fantastiques, une péripétie qui serait à l’origine du plan machiavélique de Dr Doom.
Dès lors, il paraît logique d’avoir vu la série Loki pour comprendre ce que le frère adoptif de Thor fait là, surtout dans son accoutrement du bureau du TVA. Celles et ceux qui n’auraient rien suivi depuis Avengers: Endgame pourraient vite être perdus. Un vrai danger narratif pour une réunion aussi ambitieuse. Loki est par ailleurs la meilleure série du Marvel Cinematic Universe. Un vrai argument, avant même de penser à Avengers: Doomsday.

articles.title: Fourth SharePoint Vulnerability Exploited in Past Month’s Wave of Attacks
articles.text:
The in-the-wild exploitation of yet another SharePoint vulnerability has come to light – the fourth in the past month.
The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-50522, and it was fixed by Microsoft on July 14 with its latest Patch Tuesday updates.
Microsoft describes CVE-2026-50522 as a critical remote code execution vulnerability stemming from deserialization of untrusted data.
“In a network-based attack, an attacker authenticated as at least a Site Owner, could write arbitrary code to inject and execute code remotely on the SharePoint Server,” the company wrote in its advisory.
Threat intelligence firm Defused appears to be the first to have observed exploitation of CVE-2026-50522.
The company reported on July 17 that its honeypots had seen exploitation attempts targeting what appeared to be a zero-day SharePoint vulnerability. However, in an update shared on July 20, Defused said the targeted vulnerability was likely CVE-2026-50522.
One day later, shortly after PoC exploit code was released, security firm WatchTowr confirmed active exploitation.
According to the company, threat actors are “stealing machine keys to retain long-term access”.
“Attackers are pulling SharePoint machine keys via a single request,” WatchTowr noted, adding, “Patching is not enough; defenders should rotate credentials on any assets that may have been exposed.”
Microsoft has yet to update its advisory for CVE-2026-50522 to confirm in-the-wild exploitation, but it’s not uncommon for the tech giant to delay updating its advisories after attacks are detected.
The other SharePoint vulnerabilities whose exploitation has come to light in recent weeks are CVE-2026-58644, CVE-2026-56164, and CVE-2026-45659.
CISA recently warned organizations about attacks targeting SharePoint instances. The agency’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog currently includes 13 SharePoint flaws, including five added this year. CVE-2026-50522 has not yet been added to the KEV list.

articles.title: Tesla : pourquoi la France dit officiellement non au FSD
articles.text:
Les Pays-Bas ont ouvert le bal en avril 2026, première autorité européenne à homologuer le Full Self-Driving supervisé de Tesla, ce système qui gère seul l’accélération, le freinage, les changements de voie et les intersections, en ville comme sur autoroute.
Depuis, la Lituanie, l’Estonie, le Danemark et la Belgique ont suivi. La France, elle, dit non, et comme l’ont raconté nos confrères de Numerama, ce refus n’a rien d’un simple retard administratif. Le ministre des Transports Philippe Tabarot a même publié une vidéo pour justifier sa position.
Dans cette intervention, le ministre déroule deux grandes inquiétudes : la vitesse et l’attention du conducteur. Prenons-les une par une, parce que les deux ne se valent pas.
Le procès en excès de vitesse
Premier grief : le FSD dépasserait les limitations sans que le conducteur ne demande quoi que ce soit. Tabarot cite un cas concret, une voiture qui roule à 70 km/h là où c’est limité à 50 parce que le trafic circule à cette allure, avec des écarts pouvant grimper à 50 % au-dessus de la limite. Sur le principe, il n’a pas complètement tort, et c’est justement là que ça se complique pour Tesla.
D’un côté, le système propose plusieurs profils de conduite aux Etats-Unis : le conducteur choisit lui-même son style, du plus prudent au plus pressé, et il peut toujours accélérer à la pédale pour aller plus vite. La voiture applique un réglage validé par l’humain au volant.
Sauf que dans la vraie vie, c’est plus flou, et notamment en Europe. Un journaliste d’Electrek (au Canada) a récolté une contravention à 78 km/h dans une zone à 50, en mode Standard, sans rien avoir demandé ; il souligne surtout que Tesla a retiré, dans la version 14 de son logiciel, le réglage fin qui permettait de plafonner la vitesse.
À l’inverse, sur Reddit, des propriétaires se plaignent du contraire : leur FSD colle pile à la limite et refuse d’accélérer, quitte à gêner tout le monde derrière. En Europe, il semblerait que les profils ne soient pas les mêmes qu’en Amérique.
En Belgique, le manuel officiel Tesla indique : « Vous pouvez contrôler la manière dont la Conduite entièrement automatique (supervisée) gère la vitesse de trois façons : en tournant la molette de droite du volant vers le haut ou vers le bas pour ajuster manuellement la vitesse maximale ; en définissant un décalage de vitesse maximale qui ajuste dynamiquement la vitesse maximale en fonction d’un pourcentage fixe de décalage par rapport à la limite de vitesse détectée ; en activant la vitesse maximale contextuelle, qui permet au système de s’ajuster dynamiquement en fonction des indices visuels de la scène de conduite« .
La réalité est donc bien plus capricieuse que ne le laisse entendre le ministre, dans un sens comme dans l’autre. La Suède a d’ailleurs signalé le même souci de dépassement à l’Union européenne.
Il est vrai que la possibilité pour la voiture d’ajuster dynamiquement la vitesse, sans volonté du conducteur, est précisément ce que le ministre reproche au FSD.
Le vrai sujet, c’est la responsabilité
La deuxième inquiétude porte sur l’attention : d’après les données du ministère, le FSD ne garantirait pas une vigilance suffisante en ville et dans les manœuvres délicates comme les ronds-points ou les intersections. L’argument n’est pas absurde.
Un ancien responsable du programme de conduite autonome d’Uber a lui-même raconté comment un FSD trop lisse avait endormi sa vigilance juste avant un accident. Le paradoxe est connu : plus le système est bon, moins on surveille.
Mais franchement, tout ça masque le vrai point de blocage, et Tabarot le dit lui-même : même FSD activé, le conducteur reste pénalement responsable à tout moment. C’est là que se joue la partie. Tant que le cadre juridique fait porter la faute sur l’humain au volant plutôt que sur la machine, autoriser un système « mains libres » revient à ouvrir une zone grise inconfortable.
Tesla commence tout juste à bouger sur ce terrain : au Texas, le constructeur a accepté d’assumer la responsabilité en cas d’accident, mais seulement dans des cas très particuliers et pour son service de robotaxi. On est loin d’un engagement mondial.
Le FSD, plus sûr qu’un humain : oui ou non ?
Il y a enfin l’argument qui fâche : sur le papier, ces systèmes sont plus sûrs qu’un conducteur humain. Les données publiées par Tesla font état d’un accident majeur tous les 5,3 millions de miles, soit environ 8,5 millions de kilomètres, en Amérique du Nord, contre un tous les 660 000 miles pour la moyenne américaine.
Le constructeur en tire un « 7 fois plus sûr » un peu optimiste, puisqu’il compare ses propres relevés à des statistiques nationales pas tout à fait comparables ; une analyse de Forbes ramène l’avantage réel autour de deux fois mieux qu’un humain seul. Ça reste considérable. Un neurochirurgien estimait d’ailleurs que ces aides à la conduite sauvent plus de vies que la médecine.
Alors, pourquoi ça va durer ? Parce que la France ne peut pas trancher toute seule : pour valider le FSD à l’échelle des Vingt-Sept, il faut une majorité qualifiée d’États membres, et plusieurs régulateurs traînent des pieds.
Pendant ce temps, la concurrence chinoise avance : le système maison de Xpeng a bluffé des journalistes dans les rues de Munich, et mon collègue JB a même pu essayer le FSD à Paris, où il se débrouille déjà très bien.
Le ministre, lui, vise l’arrivée de véhicules réellement autonomes homologués en France en 2027. D’ici là, le FSD restera au garage : l’excès de vitesse est l’argument le plus fort du dossier.

articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – BVNK once for stablecoins | TechCabal
articles.text:
Howdy. ☀️
Expanding into new African markets sounds exciting. Doing it successfully is a different story.
Join our next Moonshot Conversation, in partnership with Grey Business, as founders and operators unpack the real cost of cross-border growth; from payments and regulations to building sustainable operations. If you’re building a startup and thinking about expanding into another African market, this conversation is for you.
Get smarter about Francophone Africa with our newsletter, Francophone Weekly—the startups, tech policies, and institutions building the pipelines for ecosystem growth.
Fintech
LemFi taps BVNK to build stablecoin-based remittance settlement
Since 2025, you’ve probably heard a lot about stablecoins, and by now you’re probably tired of them. But what exactly is a stablecoin, and why are fintechs suddenly so gung-ho about using them to move money across borders?
When you send money from London to Lagos on LemFi, the remittance app that some migrants use, you probably imagine it moving directly from one bank account to another. It doesn’t. Behind the scenes, that transfer often passes through several correspondent banks, each taking time, charging fees, and settling balances before the money reaches its destination.
LemFi wants to change that.
What’s happening? LemFi, the Nigerian-founded London-headquartered remittance fintech that said it serves over 2 million customers across the United Kingdom (UK), Europe, North America, and Australia, has partnered with BVNK, a stablecoin payments infrastructure company, to move its cross-border settlement onto stablecoin rails. Customers will continue sending pounds or dollars, while recipients still receive naira, shillings, or cedis. The only difference is what happens behind the scenes.
Explain like I’m new here: Sending money across borders involves two separate jobs. The first is moving money for customers. The second is settling balances between the financial institutions involved. That settlement layer still relies heavily on correspondent banking networks and the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT), a global remittance network, which can take days to complete because payments pass through multiple intermediary banks.
LemFi’s new system uses stablecoins to settle those balances almost instantly before paying recipients in local currency. Customers never hold or interact with crypto; it simply replaces part of the plumbing underneath the transaction.
Why this matters: World Bank data shows that sending remittances cost an average of 6.36% globally in 2025. In Sub-Saharan Africa, the average was even higher at 8.78%—almost three times the United Nations’ (UN) target of 3%. Every extra intermediary adds cost. Removing some of those steps means more money reaches families instead of payment processors.
Zoom out: This partnership builds on a strategy LemFi has been assembling over the past two years. In June 2025, it acquired UK-based credit startup Pillar to help immigrants build credit histories. In May 2026, stablecoin issuer Tether invested in the company to support stablecoin-powered remittances. Earlier this month, LemFi acquired investment platform Wealth8 to expand into wealth management. Remittances brought customers into the app. Credit, investing, and now stablecoin settlement suggest LemFi is building something much bigger than a money transfer service.
Getting paid in cedis just got easier for African businesses operating in Ghana.
Fincra now issues dedicated GHS virtual accounts to enable businesses to collect payments. See how Fincra GHS virtual accounts work.
M&A
Nedbank finally gets the keys to NCBA
Back in January, South African lender Nedbank said it wanted to buy a controlling stake in NCBA Group, one of East Africa’s largest banks. Six months later, shareholders have finally voted—and they were overwhelmingly in favour.
What’s happening? Shareholders representing 79.9% of NCBA’s issued shares accepted Nedbank’s offer, comfortably above the 66% stake the South African bank wanted to acquire. Since the offer was capped at 66%, investors who wanted to sell all their shares won’t be able to. Nedbank will still buy only 66%, leaving the remaining 34% trading on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE).
Explain like I’m new here: Buying a bank from scratch in another country is expensive, slow, and packed with regulatory hurdles. Buying an existing bank gives you customers, branches, licences, staff, and market share overnight. That’s why banks often acquire rivals instead of building from the ground up.
State of play: For Nedbank, this deal isn’t really about Kenya alone. NCBA already operates in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Rwanda, with digital banking operations in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. When it first announced the deal in January, Nedbank also said it wants to use NCBA as a launchpad into Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), two of Africa’s largest banking markets where it has little presence today.
Why this matters: African banking has entered another consolidation cycle. Building regional banks market by market is becoming less attractive than buying institutions that already have customers, licences, and infrastructure. Instead of spending years entering new countries one at a time, acquisitions let banks expand across borders in a single deal.
Zoom out: The regulators still need to give the final nod, but the hard part is largely over. If finalised by Q4 2026—as planned—the deal will create one of the biggest banking consolidations on the continent.
Download PalmPay. Bank smarter.
At PalmPay, your security is our priority. We use advanced security technology to protect your money and personal information. Bank safely and confidently with PalmPay, where every transaction is protected every time. Learn more.
Telecoms
Nigeria’s airtime lending battle ends with a split decision
If you’ve ever borrowed airtime because your balance hit zero, you might be surprised to learn that two Nigerian regulators have spent months arguing over who gets to oversee that service. A federal court has now settled the dispute.
What happened? On Monday, Justice Ambrose Lewis-Allagoa of the Federal High Court in Lagos ruled that while the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), Nigeria’s consumer protection authority, can regulate consumer protection issues around digital lending, it cannot licence telecom companies or oversee airtime lending. That responsibility now belongs solely to the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the country’s telecom regulator.
The decision ends months of regulatory uncertainty that saw major telecom operators, including MTN and Airtel, temporarily suspend airtime lending in April.
Explain like I’m new here: Airtime lending lets you borrow call credit or data when you run out and repay it later. It has become a huge business in Nigeria, generating between ₦300 billion and ₦400 billion ($217 million–$290 million) annually. At the time, the FCCPC argued that these services qualified as digital lending and approved nine airtime and data lenders, including Fonyou Technologies and ERL Telecoms. The court did not revoke those approvals, but it ruled that licencing telecom services falls under the NCC. That means the FCCPC can still step in when consumers are treated unfairly, but it cannot decide who gets to operate airtime lending services.
What changes now? For consumers, very little. Airtime lending is expected to continue—already, Airtel and Globacom resumed the service in May; MTN joined a few weeks after, but companies now have clearer regulatory direction on whose rules they must follow. The NCC remains in charge of licencing telecom services, while the FCCPC focuses on protecting consumers from unfair business practices.
Zoom out: As fintech and telecom services continue to overlap, regulators are increasingly bumping into each other’s mandates. This ruling draws a clearer line between sector regulation and consumer protection, making it easier for companies to know which regulator they answer to while reducing the risk that regulatory disputes disrupt services used by millions of Nigerians.

The theme for this year’s Naira Life Conference by Zikoko is “All About Wealth.”
Join 2,000+ in Lagos on August 22 for a day of practical money conversations and workshops designed to move you from simply earning an income to building lasting wealth. Get 15% off early bird tickets.
Telecoms
Kenya creates a new licence for telecom equipment distributors
If your business imports smartphones, routers, fibre equipment, or mobile network hardware into Kenya, there is now another form to fill before those products can enter the country.
What’s happening? Kenya’s Communications Authority (CA), the country’s telecoms regulator, has introduced a Communications Equipment Distributor (CED) licence. From now on, businesses importing or wholesaling communications equipment must obtain a CED licence before their products can be approved or cleared into Kenya. Existing Telecommunications Equipment Contractor (TEC) and Vendor Licence holders that also import equipment must switch to the new licence.
Explain like I’m new here: Kenya is separating who brings telecom equipment into the country from who installs or sells it. Previously, distributors operated under Kenya’s Unified Licencing Framework (ULF), introduced in 2016, where equipment contractors and vendors fell under broader licensing categories. Under the revised market structure gazetted in April 2026, Kenya is moving away from that decade-old framework by creating a standalone category for communications equipment distributors, separating importers and wholesale distributors from contractors and other telecom service providers.
Before a shipment can be approved, the regulator wants to know both that the equipment meets Kenya’s technical standards and that the company importing it is properly licenced.
Why now? Kenya’s telecom market has grown far beyond mobile phones. Companies are importing fibre equipment, Wi-Fi routers, enterprise networking hardware, base stations, and other communications devices at a much larger scale. By creating a separate distributor licence, the regulator gets a clearer picture of who is responsible for bringing regulated equipment into the country and can more easily enforce compliance when something goes wrong.
What changes for businesses? Getting the new licence won’t be cheap. Businesses will pay KES 250,000 ($1,900) upfront to obtain it, then an annual operating fee of 0.4% of gross turnover or KES 120,000 ($930), whichever is higher. The licence also becomes another requirement before communications equipment can move through TradeNet, Kenya’s customs platform. Businesses that ignore it risk paying fines of up to KES 1 million ($7,750), imprisonment for up to three years, or both.
Zoom out: Kenya’s telecom regulator is paying closer attention to the supply chains behind digital infrastructure. The focus is no longer just whether a device works safely, but also who imported it, distributed it, and can be held accountable if it doesn’t.

articles.title: New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves
articles.text:
New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves
Scientists have built a programmable chip that can slow light on command, potentially clearing the way for faster and far more efficient optical computers.
- Date:
- July 21, 2026
- Source:
- Seoul National University College of Engineering
- Summary:
- Scientists have created a programmable optical chip that can slow light on demand, giving engineers far greater control over how optical signals propagate through a circuit. The technology could provide the delays, synchronization, and buffering functions needed to make light-based computing more practical. A single chip could eventually perform several tasks that currently require separate devices, potentially reducing energy use, cost, and complexity in AI servers and data centers.
- Share:
Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.
The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.
Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck
The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.
These challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.
However, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.
To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.
The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.
Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait
Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information quickly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.
Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.
One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.
CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.
- Coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT): An optical phenomenon that selectively transmits and delays light within a specific frequency range through interference among multiple resonators.
- Optical resonator: A photonic device that confines or circulates light of a specific frequency for a certain period; used in signal delay, filtering, and modulation.
Fixed Optical Devices Limit Flexibility
Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.
For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.
That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever new capabilities are needed.
The problem is especially important for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.
A Programmable Design for Controlling Light
The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.
Together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.
Using the new CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.
This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.
Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape
The researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.
This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.
Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.
The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.
- Optical pulse: A short burst of light used as a basic unit for transmitting information in optical communication and computing systems.
Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical
The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.
They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.
The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.
- Silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit: A low-loss and highly stable waveguide platform widely used for optical signal processing and integrated photonic devices.
- Thermal crosstalk: A phenomenon in which heat generated in one part of a circuit affects neighboring components, potentially altering device performance.
One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions
The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.
The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.
These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.
The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.
Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers
If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.
In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.
This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.
Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.
Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.
Researchers Plan Larger Programmable Photonic Systems
Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies."
Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We plan to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation."
Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.
Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.
The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.
Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Seoul National University College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Seungkyun Park, Beomjoon Chae, Hyungchul Park, Sunkyu Yu, Xianji Piao, Namkyoo Park. Fully Programmable Slow Light Based on a Spinor Representation of Generalized Coupled‐Resonator‐Induced Transparency. Advanced Science, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/advs.76378
