articles.title: Angel investor Jesse Wiebe conditionally discharged following guilty plea | BetaKit
articles.text:
Prominent Saskatoon angel investor Jesse Wiebe has pleaded guilty to unlawfully entering a home. He received a conditional discharge and a year’s probation.
Wiebe, an active angel investor in Canada’s startup scene, was charged in June. According to court records viewed by BetaKit, in the early morning hours of May 17, Wiebe entered a residence in downtown Saskatoon while naked. Once inside, he refused to leave, despite being threatened and hit by one of the two male occupants. Wiebe was unknown to the residents at the time.
According to an agreed statement of facts entered into provincial court records, when police arrived, they found Wiebe in the hallway outside of the residence. They said he appeared to be under the heavy influence of narcotics and in a state of “excited delirium.” Police then subdued Wiebe with a directed-energy weapon (a class of less-lethal devices that include TASERs). Wiebe was treated at a hospital before being released the following day.
Wiebe launched the Canadian Startup Capital Association (CSCA) in April after leaving his longtime position at investment network Startup TNT. The CSCA is one of three organizations, alongside the National Angel Capital Organization and the Canadian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association, that hope to influence how the federal government deploys the $750-million it pledged toward “early growth-stage funding gaps.”
In an apology letter submitted to the court, Wiebe took responsibility for the incident, citing struggles with mental health and substance use as contributing factors.
“I take full responsibility for my actions that night. I was heavily intoxicated by various substances, and that is not an excuse. It is part of the problem,” Wiebe wrote to the court.
During sentencing, Provincial Court Judge Brian Huculak issued a conditional discharge to Wiebe. A conditional discharge means the court will suspend sentencing during a probationary period; if no breach of probation occurs, the court does not enter a sentence, and no criminal record is kept.
Wiebe agreed to several conditions that will apply during his one-year probation, including completing community service, abstaining from alcohol or drugs, attending counselling, and apologizing to the people whose home he entered. If he breaches those orders, he could face up to 18 months in jail under the summary charges laid against him.
BetaKit reached out to Wiebe to ask about the plea agreement, but he declined to comment.
In his letter to the court, Wiebe said he began seeing a registered social worker before the May 17 incident, and continues to see one now. He also stated he has been sober since the event occurred and is committed to remaining so.
Other letters submitted to the court on Wiebe’s behalf include character references from prominent members of Saskatchewan’s business community, like Jason Aebig, the CEO of the Greater Saskatoon Chamber of Commerce, as well as Colton Wiegers of Wiegers Financial & Benefits, and Khanh Nguyen, of Shapeshift Developments.
In his letter, Wiebe acknowledged that support.
“I am humbled that the people who know me best, and who know exactly what I am charged with, continue to trust me and stand behind me. That trust is something I take seriously,” Wiebe wrote. “I am determined to honour it.”
If you or someone you know needs help, please use these federal resources for mental health or substance abuse support. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text the 24/7 suicide crisis helpline at 988.
With files from Jesse Cole.
Feature image courtesy Jesse Wiebe.

articles.title: Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
articles.text:
Microsoft is expanding its Xbox backward compatibility efforts today by bringing original Xbox games to PC. An early preview release will see four classic Xbox games available on PC today, as part of a bigger effort to bring more Xbox console games to PC in the future.
Microsoft is bringing original Xbox games to PC
Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
Xbox backward compatibility for PC allows classic Xbox console games to officially run on Windows.
The first four games are Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy. You’ll be able to purchase and download each of these games on PC, and they’ll also be included with all Xbox Game Pass plans. If you already own a digital copy of these games, you can now play them on PC or handhelds like the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X.
Microsoft has also added a bunch of PC features to these games to make it easier to customize graphics settings while maintaining the original gameplay. VSync support has been added, alongside up to 4x resolution upscaling, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, fullscreen and windowed modes, and more.
Achievements are also coming to these four classic Xbox games in the coming months, a highly requested addition for both console and PC. All four titles will also include customizable language and audio settings.
Most modern PCs will be able to run these Xbox games comfortably, and Microsoft’s minimum system requirements include:
- GPU: Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310
- CPU: Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor
- RAM: 8GB
You will also need Windows 11 to run these original Xbox games, and Microsoft recommends a GTX 1070 Ti or equivalent on the GPU side and a six-core CPU like the Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 to get the best out of these games.
“This marks the beginning of a broader effort to preserve Xbox games from the past and bring them to PC over time,” says Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox. “Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC is another step toward preserving the games from the past and making it easier for you to enjoy and play more of the games you already own across the devices you use every day.”
Ronald first teased that classic Xbox games were coming to PC earlier this year, in a discussion about the next-generation Project Helix Xbox console. Microsoft’s next Xbox will also play PC games, and the company has been working on a disc-to-digital feature that will allow Xbox owners to digitize their existing physical game collections in preparation for future Xbox consoles.

articles.title: The National Climate Assessment is broken – appointing Matthew Wielicki to lead it won’t help
articles.text:
In early July 2026, the Trump administration quietly tapped Matthew Wielicki to lead the U.S. Global Change Research Program. The move places a podcaster known for downplaying the threats of climate change – and importantly, someone who has not been meaningfully involved in research on climate change or its impacts – at the top of one of the country’s most important scientific enterprises, one mandated by federal law.
Under the law, the Global Change Research Program – USGCRP for short – is required to prepare and submit a National Climate Assessment to the president and Congress at least every four years. Its purpose is to help the country’s businesses, communities and governments at all levels make better decisions about how to respond to the growing risks posed by climate change.
The National Climate Assessments have done two things exceedingly well since the first report was released in 2000: They have told hard truths about the risks that climate change poses to the United States, and they have made clear that, if left unchecked, those risks are going to get much worse.
But despite the best intentions and science, the assessments have largely failed to fulfill a critical aspect of their mandate: They haven’t provided decision-makers with a clear accounting of the range of national and local options for adapting to or mitigating climate risks. They have also remained largely silent on which adaptation or mitigation strategies are most appropriate in different places and under different climate scenarios. And they have said next to nothing about how to make decisions in the face of the risks – and inevitable uncertainties – posed by climate change.
This is why I have argued that the National Climate Assessment, and other climate reports like it, are broken and in urgent need of repair. I come to this conclusion from my experience as an interdisciplinary climate and decision scientist, as a member of the team that reviewed the Fourth National Climate Assessment beginning in 2017 and as chair of a National Academies working group charged with figuring out how climate reports like the National Climate Assessment could better support decision-makers in business and government.
Fixing a broken National Climate Assessment is the job of the person in charge of the USGCRP. But the fix it needs isn’t pretending that climate change isn’t happening – the evidence is everywhere in extreme downpours, deadly heat waves and severe droughts. The real fix is to expand the focus of the National Climate Assessment from just reporting the causes and consequences of climate risks to providing better advice about how to manage them.
Why sharing solutions also matters
To be fair, scientists who develop assessments like this focus on the evidence; they tend to avoid recommending particular courses of action because doing so would require making explicit value judgments that extend beyond the scientific evidence. This is a level of restraint that many people have come to expect from the scientific community.
But as the risks posed by climate change have become more acute, this omission has limited the National Climate Assessment’s usefulness for leaders in business and government who might want – or need – to use it.
Imagine learning from your doctor that you have been diagnosed with a serious illness, only to be ushered out of the office before hearing about either your treatment options or what other patients have done – and how they have fared – under similar circumstances. That’s largely the story of the National Climate Assessment. It does a terrific job of enumerating risks, but a poor job of helping people decide how – and, in some cases, even if – they should manage them.
The National Climate Assessment under Trump
Appointing Wielicki, a former geochemistry instructor and climate science critic, to lead the USGCRP and oversee the National Climate Assessment won’t address the report’s shortcomings. In fact, I expect it will make them worse.
Given the administration’s history, it’s not a stretch to imagine a USGCRP under Wielicki’s leadership soft-pedaling climate risks or, worse, amplifying the debunked “climate change is a hoax” narrative advanced by the Trump White House. Why? Because it’s already happening.
The administration dismantled the USGCRP in 2025. Then it commissioned a group of climate skeptics to write their own government report dismissing the risks of climate change, part of an effort to buttress the administration’s moves to rescind a decades-old federal finding that climate change endangers public health and welfare. A court later determined that the report was illegally produced.
At the same time, the world’s 10 hottest years on record have all happened since 2015, and Americans across the country are experiencing climate change in worsening storms, riskier floods and fires, extreme heat and drought. Leaders are looking for ways to alleviate those risks. Indeed, the long-term success of their businesses demands that they do so.
What decision-makers in business and government across the country really need isn’t deflection or denial. They need information about the costs, benefits and uncertainties associated with different climate risk-management options that they can act on.
They also need a clearer picture of the trade-offs associated with acting now, delaying action or, in some cases, choosing to do nothing.
Over time, an improved National Climate Assessment would build a searchable library of practical and relatable case studies of climate risk-management decisions. They would describe, among thousands of examples, why and how New York City used scenario planning to prepare for sea-level rise and more intense storms; why Flagstaff, Arizona, turned to a ballot initiative to address flood and wildfire risks; how places from Burlington, Vermont, to Georgetown, Texas, fared after transitioning their electricity grids exclusively to renewables; and why governments in South Florida have continued to avoid policies that would limit development or pursue managed retreat from vulnerable areas despite swelling political and scientific consensus about the long-term risks.
Cases like these are what would form the backbone of a more effective National Climate Assessment.
Providing candid, useful examples to follow
One key to making these case studies useful is to be candid about the strengths and weaknesses of competing options for managing risk, including maintaining the status quo.
Another is to provide guidance on how the lessons from each case can be adapted to different places and different kinds of risks.
An important third key is to keep these cases updated over time so users of the National Climate Assessment can learn from the outcomes of others’ decisions.
All three are well within the grasp of the USGCRP if it is operating under knowledgeable and experienced leadership.
And this brings us back to the analogy of the doctor and the patient. Some patients will opt for treatment, while others will choose to ignore their diagnosis. It’s the same story for how organizations and governments respond, or not, to climate change.
Only by developing a better understanding of how and why specific decisions to act on climate were made, and then what happened next, can those charged with managing future climate risks be better prepared to confront decisions about climate action when it’s their turn to make them.

articles.title: Glow emerges from stealth at $1.2B valuation to challenge endpoint security in the AI era | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Glow, a cybersecurity startup founded by former Meta and Snowflake executives, emerged from stealth as a unicorn, betting that artificial intelligence is reshaping how enterprises secure employee devices.
The Palo Alto-headquartered startup on Wednesday said it raised $180 million in an all-equity Series A funding round that valued it at $1.2 billion, with backing from Sequoia Capital, Cyberstarts, Greenoaks, and Redpoint Ventures, alongside participation from Index Ventures, Swish Ventures, Lux Capital, Operator Collective, and Holly Ventures. The investment made Glow one of the latest cybersecurity startups to achieve unicorn status before publicly disclosing revenue metrics.
As more enterprises deploy AI tools and attackers increasingly use generative AI to automate phishing, develop malware, and launch more sophisticated cyberattacks, companies are rethinking how they secure endpoints — from employee laptops to servers and other connected devices. Concerns have intensified since Anthropic unveiled its Mythos AI model, which the company said demonstrated advanced capabilities in identifying and exploiting software vulnerabilities, prompting broader debate over AI-assisted cyberattacks. Glow is betting that this shift requires a new approach to endpoint security.
Founded in 2025, Glow is building an endpoint security platform that helps enterprises monitor and control the software, AI agents, and developer tools running on employee devices. The startup said the platform uses specialized AI agents to continuously map enterprise environments, assess risk in real time, and enforce security policies.
“If you think of the past decade, everything was moving to the cloud and SaaS. Suddenly, AI lands on the endpoint in a way we’ve never seen,” co-founder and chief executive Roi Tiger (pictured above, center) said in an interview.
Tiger, a former Meta vice president of engineering, co-founded Glow alongside former Snowflake cybersecurity strategy head Omer Singer (pictured above, left), former Claroty vice president of research and development Ophir Arie (pictured above, right), and former Meta engineering leader Arnon Joseph. The startup’s leadership team also includes chief operating officer Emily Heath, a former chief information security officer at United Airlines and Docusign who served on the board of Wiz through its $32 billion acquisition by Google and was previously a partner at Cyberstarts.
Even though it has only just emerged from stealth, Glow said it already has paying customers across industries including healthcare, retail, and financial services. However, it declined to disclose customer names and numbers. The startup’s typical deployments, Tiger said, span tens of thousands of employee devices across global organizations.
To power the platform, Glow uses AI models from Anthropic and Google’s Gemini through Amazon Bedrock, while building its own software to provide the models with enterprise context and improve their reliability for security tasks, Tiger told TechCrunch.
Glow’s platform, Tiger said, has already prevented malicious npm packages, third-party software components used to build applications, from being installed in customer environments, identified AI agents attempting to pull in such software, and detected employee devices where endpoint detection and response tools were missing or operating with reduced functionality.
Glow enters a crowded endpoint security market dominated by companies including CrowdStrike, Microsoft, SentinelOne, and Palo Alto Networks. Tiger said existing endpoint detection and response products focus primarily on detecting threats after they emerge, whereas Glow is designed to prevent risky software, AI agents, and developer tools from entering enterprise environments in the first place.
The startup employs nearly 100 people, about 70% of whom are in Israel and the remainder in the U.S. Whether AI-native endpoint security platforms become a distinct category remains to be seen, as enterprises are only beginning to grapple with the security implications of increasingly capable AI models.

articles.title: Esta teoría sobre el Steve Rogers del tráiler de 'Avengers: Doomsday' cambiaría para siempre la película... y no te va a gustar
articles.text:
El nuevo tráiler de Avengers: Doomsday nos ha dejado por fin el primer vistazo del Doctor Doom de Robert Downey Jr. Pero también ha disparado las teorías sobre lo que está por venir. Y es que, aunque hace unos días se reveló la sinopsis oficial, aún no tenemos demasiado claro cuál será la trama exacta de la película. Ahora, una de esas teorías que ha cobrado especial fuerza hace referencia al mismísimo Steve Rogers, el personaje de Chris Evans.
El antiguo Capitán América regresa en Avengers: Doomsday, y en el tráiler llega justo al final, presentado como "un milagro" por parte de Thor. El Dios del Trueno ni siquiera acaba de creerse que pueda ser él de verdad. Y eso es precisamente lo que les pasa a muchos fans. Resulta que, a raíz del avance, una gran cantidad de seguidores aseguran que este no es el héroe de las barras y estrellas que conocemos.
El Steve Rogers del tráiler de Avengers: Doomsday sería malo. Un villano haciéndose pasar por héroe pero que en realidad no tiene buenas intenciones. Las principales pistas que dan los seguidores de esta teoría son su aspecto, completamente vestido de negro, con el pelo largo y desaliñado y con barba. Muy lejos de su estilo habitual y con el que regresó al pasado para vivir una vida tranquila junto a Peggy. De hecho, en el primer avance de la película, en el que se nos presentó a su hijo, Rogers llevaba su tradicional pelo corto y la cara totalmente afeitada.
Por tanto, el Steve Rogers del nuevo tráiler no sería el mismo, sino una versión maligna que promete dar mucha guerra en Avengers: Doomsday. Su confiada y despreocupada sonrisa al coger el Mijolnir cuando existe una amenaza tan grande ahí fuera también sería otro indicativo. La única duda es por qué es capaz de levantar el martillo de Thor si es malo. Aunque es algo que ya ha sucedido en los cómics, si bien aquel Steve Rogers maligno pudo hacerlo gracias a que el hechizo de Odín fue modificado. Quizá el Doctor Doom tenga algo que ver al respecto.
¿Steve Rogers es el Capitán Hydra?
En realidad, los rumores sobre que un Steve Rogers malo aparecería en Avengers: Doomsday llevan circulando desde hace ya mucho tiempo. Antes de que Marvel lo anunciara oficialmente, varios insiders afirmaron el año pasado que Chris Evans regresaría en la película. Y estas mismas voces sugerían la posibilidad de que no interpretaría al Capitán América que conocemos sino a una variante oscura, el Capitán Hydra.
Esta versión de Steve Rogers fue manipulada desde niño para unirse a Hydra en lugar de a los Aliados. Incluso actuó como espía, como un falso Capitán América, para servir a los propósitos de la organización nazi. Es posible que Avengers: Doomsday nos presente a este Capitán Hydra, que uniría fuerzas con el Doctor Doom como uno de sus sirvientes más leales. Un giro brutal e inesperado que entristecerá a los fans del personaje cuando le vean hacer el mal.
Avengers: Doomsday se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: OpenAI says its models escaped a sandbox and breached Hugging Face
articles.text:
OpenAI says its models escaped a sandbox and breached Hugging Face
New OpenAI models apparently did whatever it took to achieve their goal
- OpenAI researchers confirm an AI agent escaped sandbox, exploited zero‑days, and attacked Hugging Face
- Controlled experiment with GPT‑5.6 Sol showed autonomous chaining of vulnerabilities and credential theft
- Security experts call it unprecedented, urging stronger AI governance, accountability, and protection models
OpenAI has confirmed one of its AI agents broke out of a sandbox, found and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities to gain access to the open internet, and then attacked a platform.
Not just any platform too - the agent was able to breach Hugging Face, one of the biggest AI and machine learning companies on the Internet today.
The good news is that this was a controlled experiment done by white hat researchers. The bad news is that if it could be done by researchers - it could probably be done by malicious actors, too.
Whatever it takes
In a blog post explaining the incident, OpenAI revealed the experiment was part of its testing of GPT‑5.6 Sol and an “even more capable pre-release model” to see how well they would perform on the ExploitGym benchmark.
ExploitGym is a cybersecurity benchmark that measures if an AI agent can turn a known software vulnerability into a real, working exploit. OpenAI ran it in a “highly isolated environment, with network access constrained to the ability to install packages through an internally hosted third-party software that acts as a proxy and cache for package registries.”
But the models found a way through. They identified and chained vulnerabilities in the package registry cache proxy to obtain open internet access and then attacked Hugging Face, reasoning that the solutions for the ExploitGym benchmark might be found there.
“In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers,” OpenAI said.

articles.title: India's nano enterprises and the struggle for formal loans
articles.text:
India's nano enterprises and the struggle for formal loans
At MSME Sparks 2026, Misha Sharma of Dvara Research explained why India's nano enterprises remain locked away from formal credit, and outlined three policy shifts that could bring millions of invisible businesses into the financial system.
India's roughly 7.34 crore MSMEs contribute close to a third of the country's GDP, employ around 26 crore people, and account for close to half of its exports, according to a SIDBI-Crisil report published in May 2025.
But blended into that number is a far larger, far less visible sector of nano enterprises, businesses so small that they aren’t considered a distinct category under most formal lending frameworks.
At MSME Sparks 2026, in a masterclass titled ‘Financing the Invisible Enterprise: A Policy Playbook for Nano Businesses’, Misha Sharma, Head of Household Finance at Dvara Research, laid out why this segment struggles to access formal credit, and what policymakers, lenders, and ecosystem players can do to close the gap.
Nano, not just micro
There's no official definition of a nano enterprise yet; the MSME Act's classification starts at “micro”, with a turnover ceiling of up to Rs 10 crore.
Dvara Research defines nano enterprises as those with an annual turnover below Rs 1 crore. ASUSE 2023-24 data estimates there are roughly 7.3 crore such enterprises in India.
“About 88% of these are Own Account Enterprises (OAEs), run by the owner, typically with unpaid family labour, while the rest are Hired Worker Establishments (HWEs), which employ at least one worker regularly,” Sharma said.
She noted that this distinction matters because it tracks ambition: “An enterprise with even one hired worker is far more likely to have growth aspirations beyond subsistence (basic survival).”
Within both groups, most firms are very small: 98% of OAEs and 72% of HWEs have annual turnover below Rs 25 lakh, according to Dvara Research.
Sizing the opportunity and struggle
Sizing this market and understanding the formal credit demand isn't easy; nano enterprises are too scattered and informal for a single clean number. But by Dvara Research's estimate, nano enterprises could collectively need anywhere between Rs 3.9 lakh crore and Rs 16 lakh crore in credit, a gap too large for lenders to keep ignoring.
Within that, Hired Worker Establishments alone account for an estimated Rs 2.4-6.7 lakh crore. Sharma pointed out that that's the segment lenders should prioritize, as it shows more growth potential: "It is this category that we are referring to, in terms of lacking access to finance."
For a lender, the decision to extend credit to a nano enterprise comes down to two questions: is the business viable enough to repay, and is there enough information as collateral, a digital trail, formal bookkeeping, to judge that.
Sharma divided nano enterprises into three broad groups based on these two factors. The first group has neither: weak business viability and no way to prove creditworthiness. "While access to finance is a problem for the nano enterprise segment, not all nano enterprises should be accessing formal credit, because there is a segment that simply does not have repayment capacity."
The second group already has reasonable access to formal credit. For instance, microfinance borrowers who've moved from group loans to individual loans over time.
It's the third group that policy needs to focus on: businesses that are genuinely capable of repaying a loan, but still get locked out because lenders have no reliable way to verify that, due to a lack of bookkeeping, collateral, digital trail, and formal records.
“This is the group where better data and smarter underwriting could unlock loans for businesses that can repay but lack formal proof of creditworthiness,” Sharma said.
Three levers for policy
Sharma proposed three interventions to put nano businesses on the formal credit map. She began by seeking an explicit regulatory definition for the nano category, separate from micro enterprises. Without that clarity, she said, credit aimed at this segment can't even be measured, let alone tracked, and "what gets measured gets done".
Next, she called for product innovation, where lenders shift away from standardized, collateral-linked loans toward cash-flow-based underwriting and flexible risk-sharing models, an area where the Reserve Bank of India can play an enabling role.
Finally, Sharma argued for selective formalization. Rather than pushing all small firms into heavy compliance, she recommended practical near-term levers such as Udyam registration and wider UPI adoption, especially since, by Sharma's account, fewer than 5% of nano enterprises currently use any digital financial service.
Blended finance, which combines philanthropic capital with commercial funding through instruments like credit guarantees and concessional debt, is another way to bring commercial lenders into this space at scale, not just in pilots.
The message running through the session was simple: there's no single fix for nano enterprises. Some smaller, household businesses genuinely don't want or need a loan, and pushing formal credit onto every nano enterprise isn't the goal.
The real policy challenge is telling those two groups apart and designing credit solutions only for businesses that want and can use loans to grow, rather than treating all nano firms the same.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.text:
Plus besoin de prompts : Claude regarde votre écran et mémorise le travail à faire
L'assistant IA d'Anthropic peut désormais observer ce que vous faites à l'écran, retenir chaque étape et reproduire la tâche à votre place. Une seule démonstration suffit.
Anthropic a dévoilé le 21 juillet une nouvelle fonction baptisée Record a Skill au sein de Claude Cowork, l'environnement d'automatisation intégré à l'application de bureau de Claude. L'abonné enregistre son écran pendant qu'il exécute une tâche, commente ses actions à voix haute, et Claude convertit cette démonstration en un skill structuré, stocké dans une bibliothèque personnelle et exécutable à la demande.
New in Claude Cowork: teach Claude a skill.
— Claude (@claudeai) July 21, 2026
Record your screen while you do a task, talk through it as you go, and Claude turns it into a skill it can run again. Find it under Record a skill in the + menu of the Claude desktop app.
Available on Pro, Max, and Team plans. pic.twitter.com/9OgJLOKWzj
Comment fonctionne l'enregistrement de compétences
Le système capture simultanément l'activité à l'écran, les clics de souris, les frappes au clavier et le commentaire vocal. À partir de cette matière brute, Claude isole les étapes fixes, repère les données variables et déduit les conditions de réussite du flux de travail. Le skill généré prend la forme d'un fichier lisible et modifiable, sauvegardé localement. Renommage en lot de fichiers, préparation d'un rapport hebdomadaire, mise à jour d'un tableau de suivi : chaque routine enregistrée peut être rejouée sans rédiger la moindre consigne.
Une marche de plus vers l'assistant autonome
Jusqu'ici, créer un skill pour Cowork imposait de rédiger manuellement un fichier descriptif truffé de métadonnées, de consignes et de scripts : un exercice réservé aux profils techniques. Record a Skill abaisse ce seuil ; montrer vaut désormais expliquer. La fonction vient compléter un écosystème Cowork déjà doté de l'accès aux fichiers locaux, de la mémoire persistante, de connecteurs tiers et de l'agent navigateur Claude in Chrome.
Elle est accessible depuis le menu + de l'application de bureau, rubrique Record a Skill, pour les abonnés Pro, Max et Team.

articles.title: Google transforme son moteur de recherche en France : voici les Aperçus IA et le Mode IA
articles.text:
Attendu depuis son lancement mondial en mai 2024, le déploiement des réponses générées par intelligence artificielle de Google arrive enfin dans l’Hexagone. Après plusieurs années d’attente liées au cadre réglementaire français sur les droits voisins (une loi de 2019 imposant des négociations de rémunération avec les éditeurs de presse), la firme de Mountain View dit avoir débloqué la situation. Les utilisateurs français vont ainsi avoir accès à une nouvelle interface qui donne des réponses directes au lieu de simplement renvoyer vers des sites web.
Les réponses directement dans le moteur de recherche avec les Aperçus IA
Annoncés à l’origine en 2024, les Aperçus IA (AI Overviews) se présentent sous la forme de réponses qui s’affichent désormais directement tout en haut de la page après avoir fait votre recherche. L’algorithme de Google génère automatiquement un résumé structuré des résultats qu’il a trouvé sur le web (à condition que Google juge cette réponse utile), avant même d’afficher des liens vers les sites web sources. Comme toujours avec Google, le but est de vous donner la réponse le plus rapidement possible sans jamais quitter son écosystème.
C’est un changement très important pour les utilisateurs du moteur de recherche, mais aussi et surtout pour les éditeurs de contenus qui alimentent ces algorithmes. Pour calmer la gronde, des droits voisins ont été négociés avec les propriétaires de sites qui peuvent faire jouer une option d’opt-out via la Search Console, un réglage qui permet de désactiver complètement l’intégration de leurs pages au sein des résumés générés par l’IA. Suivre la vague ou être totalement écarté d’un outil qu’énormément de monde finira par utiliser, en somme.
La navigation conversationnelle avec le Mode IA
Les Aperçus IA, parfois controversés, ne sont pas la seule nouveauté, Google introduit également le Mode IA (AI Mode), une fonction conversationnelle directement intégrée à la recherche. Alimentée par Gemini 3.5, cette interface permet d’interagir par écrit, par la voix ou via des images tout en utilisant les capacités de raisonnement approfondies et les liens vers le web.
Mais contrairement à une conversation classique avec Gemini, ce Mode IA s’appuie de manière plus importante sur la recherche web en renvoyant vers du contenu Google Images, Google Shopping ou Google Actualités. L’utilisateur a ensuite la possibilité de poser des questions complémentaires directement depuis un Aperçu IA, pour avoir une discussion plus interactive avec l’IA. Les Aperçus IA et le Mode IA sont disponibles depuis ce matin, mercredi 22 juillet à 7h00.

articles.title: Karrierechancen steigern? Diese Städte lohnen sich dafür besonders
articles.text:
Karrierechancen in Deutschland: Welche Städte lohnen sich abseits der Metropolen?
2025 hat Linkedin erstmals eine Analyse mit dem Titel „Cities on the Rise“ veröffentlicht. Das Ziel: Berufstätigen in Deutschland zeigen, welche Städte und Regionen die größten Berufschancen bieten. Im Gegensatz zu anderen Rankings konzentriert sich die Plattform dabei bewusst auf kleinere Orte abseits der großen Metropolen. Denn auch andere, weniger beachtete Städte und Regionen, wachsen mittlerweile wirtschaftlich enorm.
Diese deutschen Städte sind Karriere-Hotspots
Als Grundlage für die folgende Auflistung dienen laut Linkedin „exklusive“ Daten, die „das Wachstum von Neueinstellungen, die Schaffung von Arbeitsplätzen und den Zuzug von Fachkräften in ganz Deutschland erfassen.“ In diesen Regionen sollen Berufstätige die größten Chancen haben, attraktive Stellen zu ergattern und die Karriereleiter schneller nach oben zu klettern:
- Bremen
- Heilbronn
- Metropolregion Rhein-Neckar
- Ruhrgebiet
- Tübingen
- Münster
- Düsseldorf
- Karlsruhe
- Freiburg
- Leipzig
Bremen sichert sich im Linkedin-Ranking durch einen Aufschwung im Verteidigungssektor den ersten Platz. Davon profitieren Unternehmen wie Airbus Defence, Rheinmetall und Atlas Elektronik. 10.000 Mitarbeiter:innen des Verteidigungssektors in Bremen sind laut den Daten der Plattform für etwa sieben Prozent des branchenweiten Umsatzes verantwortlich. Im Vergleich zum vergangenen Jahr rückt Bremen damit vom fünften Platz auf die Spitzenposition.
Einen noch größeren Sprung nach vorn hat in diesem Jahr Heilbronn geschafft. 2025 lag die Stadt noch auf dem neunten Platz. Prägend für die Region sind die Schwarz-Gruppe und deren Innovationspark für Künstliche Intelligenz. Das sorgt für 5.000 offene Stellen für Fachkräfte. Dazu kommt, dass auch acht Fraunhofer-Zentren, darunter die Institute für Produktionstechnik und Automatisierung sowie Arbeitswirtschaft und Organisation, in Heilbronn gebündelt werden sollen, um Wirtschaft und Wissenschaft weiter voranzutreiben.
Neuzugänge in der Liste der Karriere-Hotspots Deutschlands sind Tübingen und Leipzig. Bei Tübingen sorgt der gute Mix aus Branchen für den fünften Platz. Dort finden sich Standorte für Life Sciences, Medizintechnik, Biotech und KI. Linkedin sieht Leipzig künftig als „wichtiger Treiber des Arbeitsmarkts in Ostdeutschland“. Das liegt an geplanten Investitionen in Höhe von etwa 1,3 Milliarden Euro, um die Stadt weiterzuentwickeln – und damit neue Unternehmen anzulocken.
Matthias Bergleiter, Head of Editorial bei Linkedin News, sagt zu den Ergebnissen: „Deutschlands Zukunftsstandorte liegen längst nicht mehr nur in Berlin, München oder Hamburg. In Heilbronn, der Metropolregion Rhein-Neckar, Münster oder Karlsruhe treibt selten nur ein einzelner Konzern das Wachstum. Stattdessen ziehen dort viele mittelständische Unternehmen gemeinsam mit Hochschulen und Startups an einem Strang, bilden aus und binden Fachkräfte oft über Jahrzehnte an die Region. […] Wer hier ausgebildet wird, findet häufig direkt vor Ort eine langfristige berufliche Perspektive, ohne für den nächsten Karriereschritt in eine der etablierten Metropolen ziehen zu müssen.“

articles.title: Oracle Patches Over 1,400 Vulnerabilities With Quarterly Security Updates
articles.text:
Oracle has patched more than 1,400 vulnerabilities with its July 2026 Critical Patch Update (CPU), with a vast majority of the flaws likely identified by artificial intelligence.
According to Oracle, the latest quarterly CPU includes 1,449 security patches, addressing 1,434 unique CVEs across 334 products.
Vulnerabilities have been patched in products such as Database Server, APEX, Autonomous Health Framework, Essbase, Global Lifecycle Management, GoldenGate, NoSQL Database, Spatial Studio, SQL Developer, TimesTen In-Memory Database, Application Testing Suite, Commerce, Communications, Construction and Engineering, and E-Business Suite.
Security fixes are also available for Enterprise Manager, Financial Services Applications, Food and Beverage Applications, Fusion Middleware, Analytics, HealthCare Applications, Hospitality Applications, Java SE, JD Edwards, MySQL, PeopleSoft, Retail Applications, Siebel CRM, Supply Chain, Systems, Utilities Applications, and Virtualization.
Roughly 600 of the patches are for vulnerabilities that can be exploited remotely without authentication. Hundreds of security holes have been assigned a critical severity rating.
The highest numbers of vulnerabilities were patched in E-Business Suite (410), Fusion Middleware (355), Communications (168), and PeopleSoft (84).
Considering that external researchers have only been credited for discovering a few dozen vulnerabilities, a vast majority of the newly patched flaws were found internally, likely with the aid of AI.
Oracle revealed earlier this year that it has access to top-tier AI systems, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s most capable models, and is using them to speed up and sharpen vulnerability discovery and patching.
The company said it’s applying this AI-driven vulnerability work across its own software and services, Oracle Health, and the open source components it develops and relies on.
Organizations must install the latest patches as soon as possible, as threat actors often exploit Oracle product vulnerabilities in their attacks. Examples include the exploitation of a PeopleSoft zero-day and a recently patched EBS vulnerability.

Le HONOR Magic V6 repousse les limites du smartphone pliable avec un design distinctif et robuste, des performances photo de haut niveau et une batterie généreuse conçue pour durer.

Le Xiaomi Smart Band 11 Active devrait être disponible dans les prochaines semaines. Vous aurez le choix entre au moins 4 coloris : noir, blanc, argenté ou rose pamplemousse. Le tout pour un prix d’environ 40 euros.

articles.title: Numerama va disparaître
articles.text:
Ce matin du 22 juillet 2026, le web que nous connaissons n’est plus tout à fait le même : comme sur la quasi-totalité de la planète, Françaises et Français ont accès aux AI Overviews et AI Mode. Le déploiement n’est peut-être pas terminé et Google aura probablement des concessions à faire aux industries qu’il chamboule avec ces fonctions (toutes celles qui dépendent du web ouvert pour exister, médias inclus).
Mais il est impossible de nier cette nouvelle réalité, car l’usage de l’IA est déjà trop fort et trop diffusé : dans quelques mois, ou quelques années, une requête Google amènera une réponse dont la source vient des sites web, mais n’amène pas vers les sites web. Vous taperez des mots clefs ou une question, Google produira l’article de référence pour vous répondre avec Gemini et vous n’irez pas lire le ou les sites qui ont créé ce contenu.
C’est déjà ce que font, par millions, les utilisateurs de ChatGPT. La différence avec Google, c’est que le moteur de recherche est au cœur de la révolution du web et soutient, depuis plusieurs décennies, une économie complète basée sur l’indexation — et donc le renvoi de Google vers des sites normalement compétents sur les sujets qu’ils traitent, du blog personnel au média en passant par les fiches pratiques d’une banque ou les tuto d’un assureur.
Plusieurs études ont montré à quel point le web était sinistré après l’ouverture d’AIO dans un pays : des pans entiers d’une industrie qui s’effondrent (comme le tourisme, particulièrement touché), incapables d’encaisser une chute de trafic de 60 à 40 %. Car ces visites, ce sont des revenus publicitaires, des achats, des abonnements, des inscriptions à une newsletter, des revenus d’affiliation… bref, une véritable économie, qui emploie des centaines de millions de personnes dans le monde et fait vivre de très nombreux acteurs du web.
Il est donc tout à fait probable que Numerama, comme la plupart des sites web que vous lisez, disparaisse de Google. Le mieux que l’on puisse espérer, d’ici à quelques mois, sera une citation en source d’une AI Overview, sur laquelle vous ne cliquerez pas, vu que votre réponse générée par IA sera déjà présente sur Google. Google affirme que les AIO ont rapporté des milliards de clics aux éditeurs, mais n’affiche pas la donnée dans la Search Console, l’outil dont nous disposons pour mesurer le trafic — pratique pour communiquer comme ils l’entendent.
Anticiper l’avenir, ça vaut aussi pour nous
Difficile pourtant, pour un média comme Numerama, de jouer la surprise. Nous faisons l’analyse de la mort de ce cercle vertueux qui nourrit le web depuis bien longtemps — même avant que Google ne lance les AIO. Et comme nous allons être directement touchés par une baisse drastique de nos revenus liés au web ouvert et à son indexation, il faut regarder la réalité en face et se préparer.
Cela tombe bien, c’est précisément ce que nous avons commencé à faire et que nous allons accélérer.
Numerama est présent sur tous les canaux de distribution
Google n’existe pas que dans sa recherche. Nous sommes aussi présents sur Google News et Google Discover, qui poussent encore des articles d’actualité ou de fond. Si vous aimez notre contenu, c’est le moment de nous suivre sur ces canaux alternatifs directement présents dans les requêtes : cela ne remplacera pas vos autres médias entièrement, car le pluralisme est important, mais vous aurez un accès privilégié à nos pages et vous pourrez lire l’info technologique et scientifique qui compte vraiment.
Et si vous n’êtes pas très Google de base, sachez que nos articles apparaissent sur la page d’accueil de Firefox ou peuvent se lire directement dans l’application Cafeyn, avec laquelle nous avons un partenariat. Pour les plus old school d’entre vous (on vous adore, on s’inclut dedans), l’abonnement Numerama+ vous donne accès à un flux RSS complet, qui vous permettra de lire nos articles sur la plateforme que vous souhaitez.
Numerama n’est pas un site web
Depuis septembre 2025, nous avons accéléré la transformation de Numerama en média multiplateformes. Le site web a une grande importance, mais aujourd’hui, la majorité de nos lectures se font ailleurs : nous avons pleinement embrassé la nouvelle réalité pour les médias, qui doivent trouver le public où il est. Pas l’inverse, où nous fonçons dans le mur.
Notre production vidéo est suivi par près de 250 000 personnes sur YouTube, où nous produisons des longs formats creusés exclusifs à la plateforme, des Décode de l’actualité et des vidéos courtes pour rebondir rapidement sur les faits les plus marquants de la journée. Chloé, Nicolas, Nelly, Théotim, Lisa et moi-même incarnons cette production vidéo, qui cumule tous les mois plusieurs millions de vues.
Nos partenaires publicitaires, historiques et nouveaux venus, nous font déjà confiance et nous suivent sur ces nouveaux formats : eux aussi savent que le règne de la page vue est presque terminé et qu’une niche d’audience qualifiée a bien plus de valeur que des millions d’impressions sur une page web. Il reste encore beaucoup à faire pour diffuser ces nouveaux formats publicitaires, partenariats et opérations spéciales, mais les équipes d’Humanoid xp, notre agence de création, sont déjà en avance sur ces sujets et répondent avec des solutions clefs en main à la hauteur des transformations en cours. Si vous ne savez plus comment communiquer efficacement dans ce monde qui change vite, vous pouvez les contacter à cette adresse pour tous vos projets.
Nous sommes également présents partout où nos lecteurs ont besoin de nous : sur X, bien sûr, où les discussions sont redevenues vives et où l’actualité est la plus rapide et la plus technique, après un passage à vide. Mais aussi sur Instagram, TikTok ou WhatsApp où nous diffusons notre info différemment. Dès la rentrée 2026, ces canaux vont avoir toute notre attention et de nombreux nouveaux formats vont compléter les formats actuels : il sera possible d’y trouver des articles pensés pour ces réseaux que nous ne publierons nulle part ailleurs.
Nous construisons une partie de notre avenir sur ces plateformes qui ne dépendent pas de Google et moins des algorithmes, quoi qu’on en dise et qui, par leur volume, permettent de diversifier notre diffusion. Nous y associerons bientôt de nombreux nouveaux formats, encore jamais vus sur Numerama.
Numerama a une relation privilégiée avec ses lecteurs
La newsletter a été annoncée comme morte plusieurs dizaines de fois depuis sa création et pourtant, c’est un des formats les plus endurants sur le web. Une relation directe et privilégiée avec de petites audiences qui, chaque semaine, trouvent dans leur boîte mail du contenu exclusif, plus intime et plus travaillé. articles.title: Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought
articles.text:
Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought
- Date:
- July 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering
- Summary:
- A new study suggests the brain begins making decisions much earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that even primary sensory regions are influenced by higher brain areas through rapid feedback loops, rather than simply passing information forward. This more dynamic view of brain function could help engineers design future AI systems that think more like biological brains while using far less power.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.
Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.
Rethinking How the Brain Makes Decisions
The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.
For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.
Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.
Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.
Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.
"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking."
Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity
To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.
The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.
Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.
"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov said. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further."
What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI
The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.
Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop new technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.
"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these currently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alex G. Armstrong, Yurii Vlasov. Neural correlates of perceptual decision-making in the primary somatosensory cortex. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (18) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2514107123

articles.title: ChatFeatured secures $2 million USD to optimize your company’s chatbot reach | BetaKit
articles.text:
As AI chatbots eat up website traffic, a Toronto startup is offering a tailored service for companies to boost their visibility to consumer chatbots.
The news: Toronto-based ChatFeatured, an AI search optimization platform, announced on Wednesday that it had raised an oversubscribed, $2-million USD ($2.8-million CAD) equity pre-seed round, led by Toronto’s Storytime Capital and with participation from Garage Capital and BY Venture Partners. The startup plans to use the funding for product development, go-to-market efforts, and growing its five-person team.
ChatFeatured’s AI product aims to identify how companies are being mentioned by the world’s major chatbots, then generates a strategy to help these companies increase their visibility to consumers.
From the source: CEO Farris Nasr believes ChatFeatured could level the playing field for smaller brands as AI chatbots become a preferred search tool for many consumers.
“It used to be a David versus Goliath thing for these small businesses, and it’s almost like David and Goliath now,” Nasr told BetaKit. “We’re allowing the smaller businesses to compete more effectively against much bigger brands with the technology.”
Following the thread: At the beginning of 2025, a study by SEO marketing agency Eight Oh Two found that 37 percent of consumers used AI tools to begin a web search rather than a traditional search engine. Introducing AI into search has changed consumer behaviour, too—people were less likely to click on links mentioned in Google’s AI overviews, according to the Pew Research Center.
At the same time, more LLMs and bots may be viewing webpages than ever before. As of May 2025, more than half of the internet’s traffic came from bots, rather than humans, according to Calgary’s Koat.ai. ChatFeatured’s product helps generate content and LLM-friendly website fixes that make a brand’s web footprint as easy as possible for chatbots to pull from.
Final thought: Not all LLMs are created equal in terms of their consumer reach. Depending on the sector, some client companies will want their visibility boosted in some AI models more than others, ChatFeatured CTO Nithiiyan Skhanthan said. For example, Anthropic’s Claude is the most popular by far, especially for SaaS businesses—so much so that ChatFeatured charges an additional fee to track a company’s visibility in Claude.
Feature image courtesy ChatFeatured.

articles.title: Synthesia’s AI training platform is moving beyond videos into live coaching | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For years, Synthesia’s pitch was to use AI to help enterprises create interactive training videos, in minutes, for a fraction of the cost normally associated with developing corporate educational materials. The startup’s newest product is making a different bet — that the real moat in enterprise AI isn’t just generating content, but in proving that it worked.
On Wednesday, the British startup launched Roleplay Sessions, an interactive training product where employees can practice high-stakes conversations like sales pitches, performance reviews, and customer complaints with an AI avatar that talks back, pushes back, and then scores them against a rubric.
Roleplay is the first release under a broader “Sessions” platform Synthesia plans to expand into other formats, including job interviews and candidate screening, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.
The launch comes as enterprises take a harder look at whether their AI spend is paying off. Citing a meta-analysis of learning research, Synthesia argues that most corporate training — including, implicitly, its own core video product — stops short of actually changing behavior. The trainings tend to inform and demonstrate, but what really pushes someone into actually learning something is doing that thing, along with feedback.
“Video performs way better than text or sending out a document,” Synthesia CEO and co-founder Victor Riparbelli told TechCrunch. “But for most things, we learn the best by actually practicing something rather than just reading it.”
Roleplay also moves Synthesia into a more defensible position. The company’s avatar and voice technology are proprietary, but the underlying reasoning intelligence is OpenAI’s. By tacking on a layer that includes rubrics, performance data, and analytics, Synthesia is positioning itself less as an AI avatar company and more as a performance-management platform with a video front end.
“From a managerial executive layer, we’re seeing huge interest in mapping out the talent in their company in a way that’s been really difficult to do before,” Riparbelli said. “If you have your entire sales team practice with an AI role player, you can get very granular data on how your sales force is doing overall.”
Synthesia already has a few early Roleplay customers with scaled commercial rollouts, including “one of the top three companies by market cap in Europe, one of the top five Fortune 100, and one of the biggest recruitment companies in the world,” per a company spokesperson.
The two most popular use cases involve training sales teams and leadership — programs like practicing how to sell a product or have a difficult conversation. Much of it is soft skills training, Riparbelli said.
As with Synthesia’s main product, customers can either create their own training programs on the platform or enlist the help of Synthesia’s consultants to build a bespoke solution that relies in part on whatever training documents and context the company already has.
Roleplay is an enterprise offering for now, but the goal is to offer it more widely to small businesses, prosumers, and potentially educational institutions in the next few months as inference costs continue to fall. Riparbelli believes products like Roleplay represent the next phase of enterprise AI adoption, where companies care less about whether AI looks good in a social media demo and more about proving it generates measurable business outcomes.

articles.title: Adiós a los prompts en Claude: Anthropic cambia para siempre la forma de pedirle cosas a la IA (ahora es muchísimo más útil)
articles.text:
Uno de los mayores quebraderos de cabeza a la hora de usar la IA, son los prompts. A menudo las descripciones tienen que ser muy precisas o elaboradas para que así los modelos puedan entender correctamente lo que le queremos que hagan. Sin embargo, en muchas ocasiones la inspiración no surge o simplemente a la IA le cuesta entender lo que le pedimos. Por suerte, Anthropic ha encontrado una solución para Claude.
La compañía ha comenzado a activar en su IA una nueva función llamada "Tech Claude a Skill". Está disponible en Claude Cowork y tal y como indica su nombre, y te permite enseñarle al modelo una habilidad, pero de una forma un tanto diferente. En vez de añadir una descripción de texto, puedes usar la grabación de pantalla de tu dispositivo y la voz mientras completas la tarea tú mismo. Claude se quedará con todo el proceso, lo aprenderá y lo guardará como una habilidad para usarla siempre que lo necesites.
Por ejemplo, si quieres que Claude aprenda a crear informes en base a tus facturas u ordenar archivos de una manera predeterminada, en vez de escribirle lo que tiene que hacer, simplemente lo grabas mientras explicas lo que estás haciendo, como si estuvieses hablando con un humano. Lo interesante de esta función es que la memoria de Claude se queda con este proceso y lo hará siempre que sea necesario. Por tanto, no tendrás que escribir y decirle "hazlo exactamente como la última vez" cuando le vuelvas a pedir una tarea.
Cómo usar la nueva función de Claude
Anthropic ha comenzado a activar "Tech Claude a Skill" en la sección de Claude Cowork, el asistente de IA que opera de forma autónoma directamente en tu ordenador. Para activarla y enseñarle a la IA a hacer algo grabando el proceso, solo tienes que ir a la sección Cowork, pulsar en el botón '+' que aparece en el cuadro de texto y escoger la opción de 'Grabar una habilidad'. Por último, graba la pantalla y narra lo que quieres que haga la IA. Así de sencillo.
Eso sí, este añadido de Claude está disponible para los suscriptores Pro, Max y Team, por lo que necesitas pagar por alguno de estos planes para poder utilizar la función. Además, y al menos por el momento, solo está disponible en la versión para escritorio, que es donde Cowork tiene más sentido.

articles.title: What the sudden demise of the UK’s department of science means for the future of research
articles.text:
The obituaries were being written before the body was cold. Within hours of Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirming that Whitehall’s responsibilities for science and technology would be absorbed into a new Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), Sir Paul Nurse, president of the Royal Society, was on Radio 4 warning that “science isn’t a slave to business”. The trade association TechUK declared it “the wrong change at the wrong time”.
You might imagine that something ancient, ineffable and essential to British science had been ripped away. In fact, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) was only born in February 2023 – a surprise late tweak to the machinery of government under Rishi Sunak’s faltering premiership.
Science has never enjoyed a settled home in Whitehall. For most of the period from 1995 to 2023, it sat precisely where Burnham has put it now: inside a business super-department. Notably, the single most important protection UK science secured in that era – a ring-fenced budget through the George Osborne austerity years – was won from inside the Business, Innovation and Science department, under then-business secretary Vince Cable.
The historian David Edgerton has long argued that Britain’s fondness for tinkering with the machinery of government is a form of displacement activity. What actually shapes the fortunes of research is money, people and demand for what they produce, not the nameplates on London’s Victoria Street.
On that test, the outlook for science is far calmer than some reactions to this latest move would suggest. Under plans published last October, the UK’s total research and development budget is locked in at £58.5 billion over the four-year spending review to 2030 – a real-terms increase.
Machinery changes move budget lines across departments; they don’t unravel them. As yet, nothing we’ve heard from the Burnham government suggests the settlement for UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) is at risk.
A US wrecking ball
If we want to be reminded what real damage to a science system looks like, we only need to glance across the Atlantic. While London rearranges the departmental furniture and dishes out new email addresses, Washington is taking a wrecking ball to the foundations of its public science system.
A 2027 budget request will halve the size of the US National Science Foundation, if passed. A draft White House rule, due to take effect in October, will hand political appointees the power to vet federal research grants against “the president’s priorities” and terminate awards mid-stream.
A predictable exodus has begun. The Nobel laureate Omar Yaghi has just left the University of California, Berkeley for Tsinghua University in China.
Set against political commissars patrolling the borders of knowledge, the UK’s science soap opera feels deeply provincial – a debate about which secretary of state sponsors oversight of a gradually swelling budget.
And the institutional layer beneath this is in better shape than doomsayers allow. UKRI’s new strategy has set a clear five-year path: priority programmes in AI, quantum and clean energy, faster funding decisions, and a welcome seriousness about experimentation with the modes and means by which we manage public investment in research.
Not everyone is happy with UKRI’s approach to prioritisation. But a funder with a published strategy, agreed budget and hard targets is a more durable asset than a three-year-old ministry. The research councils have outlasted every department that ruled over them, and UKRI will outlast this too.
Nor should the science community be spooked by closer proximity to business. When I leave my office at UCL and stroll down the Euston Road through London’s Knowledge Quarter – dubbed “the new square mile” – I pass by the Wellcome Trust, the Crick and Turing institutes, the British Library, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. Day in, day out, this dense weave of labs, firms and cultural institutions delivers what the triple helix of government, industry and academia is all about.
And we can find versions of the same story unfolding in Manchester, Sheffield, Cambridge and Glasgow. Rather than science being subordinate or “enslaved”, the UK’s world-leading universities have spent the past decade aligning themselves with agendas for regional growth and frontier technologies.
But there’s a harder truth lurking here too. Public money accounts for less than a third of UK research and development investment. The rest is financed and largely performed by the private sector.
UK science’s chronic weakness has never been the quality of publicly funded research. It is the R&D intensity of UK firms, and their ability to convert discoveries into products, services and revenue streams generated and owned in the UK.
If yoking science to industrial strategy in a single department reminds Whitehall to treat these as a single problem, some good may come of Burnham’s reorganisation.
AI policy concerns
With DSIT’s disappearance, a particular source of concern has been the future of AI policy. This at a time when the radical possibilities and risks of AI frontier models, fluctuating US export controls, and the latest “Sputnik moment” jolt from China’s Kimi K-3 demand sustained and technically fluent policy attention.
We are also seeing a sharp acceleration in the ways AI is transforming science itself – whether by cracking mathematical problems that stumped humans for the past 87 years, or collapsing decades-old models of grant writing and peer review.
Splitting AI from science just as they converge in practice would have been the least defensible element of this reorganisation. So it is reassuring that cross-government oversight of AI, including the AI Security Institute and AI public sector adoption, is moving to a new “AI taskforce” in the Cabinet Office – alongside the promotion of Kanishka Narayan to the status of AI minister attending Cabinet. Much now rests on his shoulders.
Government departments come and go. Those of us who have long advocated for research policies built on evidence rather than gut can allow ourselves a wry smile at the fuss created by this latest reorganisation – and then get back to work.
DSIT is dead, but UK science will be fine. Keep your eyes on the AI prize – and be thankful we are arguing about organograms, not survival.

articles.title: Xiaomi assure que son robot humanoïde est presque aussi adroit qu'un ouvrier automobile
articles.text:
Cela fait quatre ans que les industriels promettent des humanoïdes au travail dans leurs usines, à grand renfort de vidéos spectaculaires et de déploiements réels au compte-gouttes. Xiaomi vient de verser sa pièce au dossier. Le 14 juillet, son fondateur Lei Jun a publié sur Weibo un plan-séquence de 45 minutes montrant son robot CyberOne à l’œuvre dans l’usine automobile du groupe, à Pékin.
 
Quatre mois d’apprentissage pour visser un écrou
La tâche confiée au robot n’a rien d’un numéro de cirque : poser des écrous autotaraudeurs, en travail double face, sur les lignes des SU7 et YU7. D’après les chiffres avancés par le groupe, le taux de réussite serait passé de 90,2 % à 98 % en quatre mois d’ajustements, à un point du niveau d’un opérateur humain. La machine aurait tenu trois heures d’affilée sans intervention, au rythme réel de la chaîne : un véhicule toutes les 76 secondes. Deux corvées annexes complètent le tableau (tri de panneaux de console, pliage de bacs de pièces), autour de 90 % de réussite chacune.
Lire aussi : Un robot tient 8 heures en usine chez Siemens : voilà la vraie percée en robotique
Lei Jun qualifie lui-même ses machines de « stagiaires », pas encore titularisées. L’aveu a le mérite de la franchise, mais n’absout la communication de critiques : tous ces chiffres sortent de la communication de Xiaomi, plan-séquence promotionnel compris, sans la moindre vérification indépendante. Le conditionnel n’est pas une coquetterie ici. Pour mémoire, CyberOne avait été dévoilé en août 2022 (1,77 mètre, 52 kilos, un prototype estimé autour de 100 000 dollars), avant de retourner au laboratoire pendant près de quatre ans.
Tesla, Figure, AgiBot : l’usine se remplit de stagiaires
Xiaomi rejoint une file d’attente déjà bien garnie : Tesla peaufine son Optimus, quand Figure est passé des lignes de BMW à la logistique, avec des sessions de plus de vingt heures d’affilée. Le Chinois AgiBot revendique de son côté 64 heures en continu sur une ligne d’assemblage de tablettes. La nuance, et elle compte : la plupart de ces démonstrations tournent sur des postes aménagés pour l’exercice, quand Xiaomi affirme opérer en conditions réelles, cadence comprise. Affirmation, là encore, invérifiable de l’extérieur.
Les chiffres de la Fédération internationale de robotique donnent l’échelle du basculement : 542 000 robots industriels installés dans le monde en 2024, dont 295 000 en Chine, plus de la moitié du total. L’Europe, elle, en a installé 85 000, en recul de 8 %, dont 23 000 pour la seule industrie automobile. Xiaomi annonce déjà vouloir déployer « un grand nombre » de ces machines dans ses usines au cours des cinq prochaines années. Pour l’ouvrier européen, la question n’est plus de savoir si la concurrence arrive, mais à quelle vitesse.
Reste l’angle mort des 45 minutes de vidéo : ce que deviendront les collègues humains le jour où le stagiaire sera titularisé.

articles.title: Adeus, iPhone? Google cria migração mais fácil para Android
articles.text:
O Google anunciou uma nova experiência de migração para quem pretende trocar um iPhone por um celular Android. A ferramenta, integrada ao Android 17, permite transferir mais tipos de dados sem instalar aplicativos extras.
A novidade amplia as opções para usuários que querem mudar de sistema, tornando o processo de transferência mais direto.
Android 17 amplia transferência de dados do iPhone
Ao trocar de smartphone, muitos usuários se preocupam em manter arquivos e informações pessoais no novo aparelho. Pensando nisso, o Google adicionou novos tipos de dados ao processo de migração entre iPhone e Android.
A transferência pode ser feita sem fio e dispensa o download de um aplicativo separado. Além de fotos, vídeos e contatos, a ferramenta agora também aceita informações que antes exigiam configurações adicionais.
Entre os dados que podem ser transferidos estão:
- fotos e vídeos armazenados no iPhone;
- contatos, mensagens e calendários;
- conta Google do usuário;
- senhas e credenciais de redes Wi-Fi;
- eSIM, o chip virtual usado em smartphones recentes.
O Google afirma que a ampliação desses recursos ajuda a reduzir as dificuldades encontradas por quem decide trocar de plataforma.
Recurso chega primeiro a Pixel e Galaxy
A novidade já começou a ser liberada para alguns dispositivos Pixel. O recurso também estará disponível nos novos Galaxy Z Flip 8 e Galaxy Z Fold 8, apresentados durante o Galaxy Unpacked.
Segundo a empresa, a ferramenta será disponibilizada para mais aparelhos Android em breve.
A integração ao sistema elimina uma etapa que costumava exigir soluções externas e permite que informações importantes acompanhem o usuário durante a configuração do novo celular.
Mudança facilita disputa entre Android e iPhone
A nova experiência de migração inclui dados essenciais da rotina digital, como mensagens, senhas e redes Wi-Fi salvas. O suporte ao eSIM também entra na lista, acompanhando a adoção desse formato em smartphones atuais.
Ao simplificar a transferência, o Google tenta diminuir um dos pontos que podem pesar na decisão de quem considera abandonar o iPhone.
A atualização do Android 17 mostra que a disputa entre os sistemas móveis não depende apenas de hardware e recursos, mas também da facilidade oferecida ao usuário no momento de trocar de aparelho.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: OpenAIs KI greift Hugging Face an: So lief die Cyberattacke durch Agenten ab
articles.text:
Interner Test eskaliert: OpenAI-Modelle hacken sich aus der Sandbox und greifen Hugging Face an
Viele KI-Modelle werden vor ihrer Veröffentlichung in Sandbox-Systemen getestet. Dadurch soll sichergestellt werden, dass die Agenten keinen Schaden auf den eigentlichen Systemen anrichten oder sich Zugang zum Internet verschaffen. Erst in jüngster Vergangenheit haben Sicherheitsforscher:innen gewarnt, dass KI-Modelle in der Lage sind, aus solchen Sandbox-Umgebungen autonom auszubrechen. Jetzt gibt es einen Fall, der das unter Beweis stellt.
Wie OpenAIs KI ausgebrochen ist
Laut OpenAI fand der Vorfall vor wenigen Tagen statt. Hugging Face hatte einen Angriff auf die eigene Infrastruktur festgestellt. Ein KI-Agent hatte versucht, sich Zugriff auf interne Systeme zu verschaffen, und wurde von den Verantwortlichen gestoppt. Nachdem OpenAI Untersuchungen angestellt hatte, stellten sie fest, dass für den Sicherheitsvorfall eine Reihe von OpenAI-Modellen verantwortlich waren, darunter GPT-5.6 Sol.
Bei der Version von GPT-5.6 Sol soll es sich um ein Pre-Release-Modell gehandelt haben, das „noch leistungsfähiger“ war. Um festzustellen, wie leistungsfähig das Modell ist, hat OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol in eine Sandbox-Umgebung verfrachtet und zusammen mit den anderen Modellen darum gebeten, „fortgeschrittene Exploits mit komplexen Angriffswegen“ zu nutzen. Für den Test wurden die normalerweise gesetzten Richtlinien, an die sich die Modelle halten müssten, aufgehoben.
Die Modelle versuchten, aus der Sandbox auszubrechen und Zugriff auf das Internet zu bekommen. Obwohl selbige eigentlich vom Internet abgeschottet war, konnten die Modelle eine Zero-Day-Schwachstelle identifizieren, sich selbst mehr Rechte zuweisen und schließlich auf dem System eine Schnittstelle zum Internet identifizieren und nutzen.
Im Anschluss einigten sich die Modelle darauf, dass Hugging Face möglicherweise die nötigen Daten für eine Lösung der Aufgabe bereithalten würde. Also versuchten sie, Zugriff auf die Seite und die dahinterliegenden Systeme zu erlangen. Dafür nutzten sie mehrere aneinandergereihte Angriffe inklusive einiger Zero-Day-Schwachstellen. Zudem verschaffte sich die OpenAI-KI Zugang zu gestohlenen Login-Daten.
Was OpenAI aus dem Vorfall lernt
Wie OpenAI betont, arbeitet das KI-Unternehmen eng mit Hugging Face zusammen, um alle Details des Vorfalls zu untersuchen. Alle Zero-Day-Lücken, die durch die KI-Agenten aufgedeckt wurden, hat OpenAI mittlerweile an die Entwickler:innen der jeweiligen Systeme weitergeleitet und arbeitet mit ihnen ebenfalls an Lösungen. Bis selbige bereitstehen, sollen sämtliche interne Tests zur Cybersicherheit von KI-Modellen vorerst verlangsamt werden.
Künftig will OpenAI noch weitere Sicherheitsmaßnahmen für seine Systeme und Modelle implementieren, um solche Vorfälle zu verhindern. Hugging Face schreibt dazu in einem Statement, dass es mittlerweile nicht mehr ausreicht, Onlineplattformen auf herkömmliche Weise zu schützen. Da die Kosten und das Skill-Level für großangelegte Angriffe auf Systeme mittlerweile durch KI gesenkt wurden, muss auch in der Verteidigung solcher Systeme Künstliche Intelligenz zum Einsatz kommen, um „mithalten zu können.“

L’interdiction des réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans a été définitivement adoptée
articles.text:
Alors que l’Assemblée nationale et le Sénat défendaient deux approches différentes pour interdire les réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans, une commission mixte paritaire était parvenue à un compromis. Ce mardi 21 juillet, le Parlement a définitivement adopté la proposition de loi visant à interdire l’accès aux réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans. Son entrée en vigueur est fixée pour septembre. Il s’agit d’une première en Europe. Néanmoins, il reste à voir comment les plateformes contrôleront l’âge des utilisateurs.
L’interdiction des réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 officiellement adoptée
Le gouvernement français était entré dans une véritable course contre la montre depuis maintenant plusieurs semaines. Pour rappel, l’Assemblée nationale voulait imposer une interdiction large des réseaux sociaux concernés, tandis que le Sénat préconisait une approche plus restreinte, craignant notamment un problème de compatibilité avec le droit européen, et plus précisément le Digital Services Act (DSA). Justement, la Commission européenne a émis des réserves sur la proposition de l’Assemblée nationale, avant que des experts européens préconisent un seuil à 13 ans. Nous étions donc face à une bataille politique à quelques semaines de la rentrée, mais un nouvel accord était venu davantage concrétiser le projet de loi.
En effet, une commission mixte paritaire réunissant députés et sénateurs a réussi à trouver un compromis : le principe d’une interdiction générale défendu par l’Assemblée nationale est retenu, tout en tenant compte des préoccupations exprimées par le Sénat. Il ne restait plus qu’à adopter le texte, et c’est maintenant chose faite. En effet, ce mardi 21 juillet, les deux chambres du Parlement ont définitivement adopté la proposition de loi visant à interdire l’accès aux réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans. Le texte a été approuvé par 243 voix contre 2 au Sénat, puis par 279 voix contre 81 à l’Assemblée nationale.
Sur X, Emmanuel Macron, qui se positionne comme le leader d’un mouvement qui vise à interdire les réseaux sociaux aux plus jeunes, s’en est bien entendu félicité : « Je m’y étais engagé, c’est désormais voté : les réseaux sociaux seront interdits aux moins de 15 ans à la rentrée. Merci aux parlementaires. Au Conseil constitutionnel de statuer puis place à l’action pour rendre cette mesure concrète et protéger nos enfants en ligne ». Pour être plus précis, les moins de 15 ans ne pourront plus créer de nouveaux comptes à partir de la rentrée. En ce qui concerne les comptes existants, ils bénéficieront d’un délai de quatre mois avant d’être désactivés. L’Union européenne devra toutefois encore examiner le projet de loi, mais le texte a maintenant été officiellement adopté. Notons enfin que l’interdiction des téléphones portables déjà en vigueur dans les écoles et les collèges sera étendue aux lycées .
Comment la vérification d’âge sera-t-elle effectuée ?
Il s’agit sans doute du point le plus sensible du dossier. La nouvelle loi veut obliger les plateformes à mettre en place des systèmes de vérification fiables de l’âge, approuvés par l’autorité française de protection des données. Mais comment vérifier l’âge d’un utilisateur sans récolter des données, qu’elles soient personnelles ou biométriques ? Le gouvernement français n’approuverait sans doute pas un système d’analyse de la structure osseuse des utilisateurs, comme Meta le propose, mais il ne propose pas non plus de solution concrète. L’application de vérification de l’âge de l’UE ou un système de vérification via une pièce d’identité restent les deux possibilités les plus probables à l’heure actuelle.
